practices.name: Amazon six-page narrative memo with silent reading
practices.source: Jeff Bezos, 2017 Letter to Shareholders (Amazon SEC filing, Exhibit 99.1)
practices.what_is_shown: Decider reads a full narrative document (not slides) at the start of the meeting, in silence, in a 'study hall'; then discussion. Order inside the memo is not fixed by the letter; the point is connected prose instead of bullets. Memo is unsigned (from the whole team).
practices.form: Text structure: narratively structured prose, max ~6 pages, read in-meeting
practices.decision_types: High-stakes, cross-functional, non-routine decisions where reasoning quality matters more than speed; familiar recurring business reviews also use it
practices.concrete_example: Bezos: a great memo is written and re-written, shared with colleagues, set aside for days and edited again; it 'might take a week or more', not one or two days.
practices.fails_when: Writer underestimates scope (written in a day, quality 'varies widely'); readers cannot recognize a great memo because the standard is hard to specify; too slow for reversible decisions.

practices.name: Amazon PR/FAQ (Working Backwards)
practices.source: Colin Bryar and Bill Carr (ex-Amazon), Working Backwards PR/FAQ Instructions & Template
practices.date: undated page (process used at Amazon since ~2004-2005)
practices.what_is_shown: Order: heading (product name) -> subheading (who the customer is, what benefit, one sentence) -> summary paragraph with launch date -> customer problem -> solution vs today's alternatives -> spokesperson and hypothetical customer quote -> how to get started. Then External FAQ (customer/press questions), then Internal FAQ (TAM, unit economics, upfront investment, dependencies, legal, 'what assumptions need to be true', 'top three reasons this will not succeed').
practices.form: Text: 1-page mock press release + FAQ, about six pages total; reviewed with 15-20 min silent reading then ~40 min discussion
practices.decision_types: New product / big-bet go/no-go decisions with high uncertainty about customer value; funnel of many ideas
practices.concrete_example: Fulfillment by Amazon used two PR/FAQs (seller view and buyer view); AWS team spent over a year revising PR/FAQs before launching S3 and EC2. Template example: Phoenix 400 SUV PR discarded as undifferentiated; Excel 850 PR kept as a destination worth solving for.
practices.fails_when: Used to 'sell' instead of truth-seek; competition or current solutions discounted; great product for the wrong problem (authors cite Fire Phone); teams resent weeks of writing before building.

practices.name: One-way vs two-way door (Type 1 / Type 2) decision triage
practices.source: Jeff Bezos, 2015 Letter to Shareholders; 2016 Letter (70% information, disagree and commit)
practices.what_is_shown: Before any content: classify the decision as irreversible (Type 1: methodical, slow, consultation) or reversible (Type 2: fast, by high-judgment individuals or small groups). 2016 letter adds: most decisions should be made with about 70% of the information you wish you had; 'disagree and commit'.
practices.form: Classification rule that sets process weight; no document format of its own
practices.decision_types: Meta-level: chooses how heavy the decision document and review should be
practices.concrete_example: Bezos: 'If you walk through and don't like what you see on the other side, you can't get back to where you were before' (Type 1); a suboptimal Type 2 decision can be reopened.
practices.fails_when: Large organizations apply the heavy Type 1 process to Type 2 decisions -> slowness, risk aversion, too few experiments; the opposite error (light process on Type 1) kills companies before they get large (Bezos footnote).

practices.name: Google design doc
practices.source: Malte Ubl (ex-Google), Design Docs at Google
practices.what_is_shown: Order: context and scope (objective facts only) -> goals and non-goals -> the actual design (overview first, then details; system-context diagram, API sketch, data storage) -> alternatives considered (trade-offs of each and why rejected) -> cross-cutting concerns (security, privacy, observability).
practices.form: Informal text in Google Docs with comment threads; system-context diagram where useful; rarely code
practices.decision_types: Ambiguous or contentious technical designs where early review is cheaper than rework; not for obvious implementations
practices.concrete_example: Non-goal example: 'ACID compliance' for a database design is stated as a non-goal, not a negated goal. Length: 10-20 pages for larger projects, 1-3 page 'mini design doc' for incremental work.
practices.fails_when: Doc is really an implementation manual with no trade-offs; overhead clashes with rapid prototyping; heavy review meetings stall progress; doc not updated after implementation (becomes 'constitution with amendments').

practices.name: Uber RFC with domain-specific templates and named approvers
practices.source: Gergely Orosz (ex-Uber), Scaling Engineering Teams via RFCs: Writing Things Down
practices.date: undated in fetched page (approx. 2019, not verified)
practices.what_is_shown: List of approvers first, then abstract, then template sections reviewers kept asking about. Backend: architecture changes, SLAs, dependencies, load testing, multi-datacenter, security, testing and rollout, metrics, support. Mobile/web adds UI and UX, network interactions, accessibility, analytics.
practices.form: Short written plan, emailed to all engineers (later per-domain lists), anyone may comment; approval recorded in writing
practices.decision_types: Any non-trivial engineering project; scales from tens to low thousands of engineers
practices.concrete_example: A team in India pointed out localization gaps in a US team's RFC before build; templates grew an accessibility section when it became a mobile focus.
practices.fails_when: Noise at thousands of engineers needs tooling and filters; templates ossify; approvers do not actually read unless required to confirm in writing.

practices.name: Rust RFC template
practices.source: rust-lang/rfcs 0000-template.md
practices.what_is_shown: Summary (one paragraph) -> Motivation with concrete use cases -> Guide-level explanation (as if already shipped, taught by example) -> Reference-level explanation (corner cases by example) -> Drawbacks ('why should we not do this?') -> Rationale and alternatives (incl. impact of not doing it) -> Prior art -> Unresolved questions -> Future possibilities.
practices.form: Markdown text in a public pull request; example-driven
practices.decision_types: Public, hard-to-reverse language/API/policy changes with many stakeholders
practices.concrete_example: Guide-level section must show sample error messages or migration guidance so the reader sees the change from the user's seat before the technical detail.
practices.fails_when: Long open threads with many commenters; 'future possibilities' mistaken for justification (template warns it is not a reason to accept).

practices.name: Oxide RFD (Request for Discussion) with explicit states
practices.source: Jess Frazelle, Bryan Cantrill, RFD 1: Requests for Discussion (Oxide Computer)
practices.what_is_shown: Metadata first (authors, state, discussion link, labels). State machine: prediscussion -> ideation -> discussion -> published -> committed / abandoned. Content asks for viable options with benefits and drawbacks, reasoning with data, the determination, plus economic, customer, performance and security impacts.
practices.form: AsciiDoc/Markdown in git branch; discussion in a pull request; 3-5 business days for comments
practices.decision_types: Technical and company-process decisions; options-survey RFDs separate from determination RFDs
practices.concrete_example: RFD 9 surveys how each cloud provider does networking neutrally; RFD 21 and RFD 63 build on it to give the reasoning and final determination.
practices.fails_when: Merged with nobody having read it (RFD 1 says ask someone explicitly); urgency forces less rigor; ideation docs that are not narrowly defined rot.

practices.name: Architecture Decision Record (Nygard ADR)
practices.source: Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions (Cognitect)
practices.what_is_shown: Title (short noun phrase) -> Context (forces in tension, value-neutral facts) -> Decision ('We will ...', active voice) -> Status (proposed / accepted / deprecated / superseded with link) -> Consequences (positive, negative and neutral).
practices.form: 1-2 page text file in the repo, numbered, never reused; full sentences, bullets only for visual style
practices.decision_types: Architecturally significant decisions whose rationale future people will need; log of many medium decisions over time
practices.concrete_example: 'ADR 9: LDAP for Multitenant Integration'; a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded, not deleted.
practices.fails_when: Nobody outside the repo reads it (Nygard notes the objection); consequences listed only as positives; written after the fact as justification.

practices.name: MADR (Markdown Any Decision Record) with option pros/cons
practices.source: adr.github.io MADR project (Kopp, Armbruster, Zimmermann)
practices.what_is_shown: Title -> context and problem statement (often as a question) -> decision drivers -> considered options (list) -> decision outcome 'Chosen option X, because ...' -> consequences (Good, because / Bad, because) -> confirmation (how compliance will be checked) -> pros and cons per option -> more info (when to revisit). Optional frontmatter: decision-makers, consulted, informed.
practices.form: Markdown template; full, minimal and bare variants
practices.decision_types: Any decision with several realistic options; small to medium, logged in repo
practices.concrete_example: 'Use Plain JUnit5 for advanced test assertions' - options JUnit5, Hamcrest, AssertJ; chosen JUnit5 because the others' features do not outweigh a new dependency.
practices.fails_when: Option lists padded with straw men; no revisit trigger; becomes bureaucracy for trivial choices.

practices.name: Atlassian DACI decision page
practices.source: Atlassian Team Playbook: DACI Decision-Making Framework
practices.what_is_shown: Title 'DACI: [question]?' -> roles (Driver, single Approver, Contributors with voice not vote, Informed) -> details (status, impact, due date, outcome) -> 1-2 sentence background -> relevant data -> decision factors (cost, time, scalability) -> options table (description, pros, cons, cost/resources) -> action items -> outcome shared.
practices.form: Confluence page with options comparison table
practices.decision_types: Complex, cross-functional, resource allocation decisions with several stakeholders
practices.concrete_example: Choosing a new project management tool: options in a table scored on cost and time; Approver decides; Informed teams (sales, support) are notified.
practices.fails_when: Roles alone do not produce good decisions (McKinsey 2019 found clear roles 'not sufficient to win' for cross-cutting decisions). Note: the page claims a McKinsey survey found 25% higher success with DACI; the cited McKinsey PDF does not mention DACI.

practices.name: Stripe team decision logs
practices.source: Brie Wolfson (ex-Stripe), Writing In Public, Inside Your Company (The Kool-Aid Factory)
practices.what_is_shown: A running record of decisions affecting the team, posted where the team communicates (Slack) and kept in a wiki; meeting notes in three sections: decisions, actions, personal commentary. Bias to over-log at first.
practices.form: Short log entries in chat + wiki; opt-in notification keyword
practices.decision_types: Frequent small and medium team decisions (often reversible) that others need to know about
practices.concrete_example: Many of Stripe's product/engineering teams posted even small decisions into team Slack channels; pushback is treated as a chance to explain the why.
practices.fails_when: Log without the why becomes noise; invites relitigation if trust is low; no outcome review. Only an ex-employee account, no official Stripe template found.

practices.name: Netflix informed captain, farming for dissent, disagree then commit
practices.source: Netflix Culture Memo
practices.what_is_shown: One named informed captain per significant decision; captain actively seeks opposing views (weighted by expertise); after the decision everyone commits; after impact is clear the captain reflects on what worked.
practices.form: Process rule plus internal memos people can comment on; no fixed document template
practices.decision_types: Significant decisions in a decentralized org ('highly aligned, loosely coupled'); avoids committee decisions
practices.concrete_example: On a creative decision, opinions of people in TV, film or games weigh more than an engineer's, and the reverse for product/technology.
practices.fails_when: Dissent farming becomes a ritual after the decision is effectively made; 'context not control' mistaken for hands-off management (memo warns).

practices.name: BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front)
practices.source: US Army Regulation 25-50 (Army writing standard); US Air Force Tongue and Quill AFH 33-337
practices.date: AR 25-50 (2013 version cited); Tongue and Quill current
practices.what_is_shown: First sentence/paragraph: the main point, the requested action and deadline; then essential background and the considerations that led to it. Email subject keywords (ACTION, DECISION, INFO, REQUEST) state what the reader must do.
practices.form: Text structure for memos and email; one opening paragraph
practices.decision_types: Time-pressured readers, routine approvals, status with an ask; any message where the reader must act
practices.concrete_example: 'BLUF: I need you to approve both the design and content of the attached flyer by noon on August 10.' then context.
practices.fails_when: A single bottom line hides uncertainty and second-order effects (policy-memo guidance says to include them in the BLUF); writer lacks mastery to compress; conclusion without justification invites rubber-stamping.

practices.name: Completed staff work (decision package for approve/disapprove)
practices.source: Col. Archer J. Lerch, 'Completed Staff Work', Army and Navy Journal (reproduced by GovLeaders; IBM/Watson copy)
practices.what_is_shown: The chief receives a finished solution in a single document ready for signature, so all that remains is approval or disapproval; alternatives and coordination are done by staff; explanation only if the chief asks. Modern US agency decision memos end with Approve / Disapprove / Discuss lines (e.g. USDA NRCS decision memo, seen only in search snippet).
practices.form: Single finished document (memo to be sent / signed) plus approval line
practices.decision_types: Hierarchical delegation; decisions the chief must own but should not work out
practices.concrete_example: 'Writing a memorandum to your chief does not constitute completed staff work, but writing a memorandum for your chief to send to someone else does.'
practices.fails_when: Hides rejected options and uncertainty (chief only sees the winner); staff pre-decides value trade-offs that belong to the chief; rough draft used to shift work back.

practices.name: Commander's intent (purpose, key tasks, end state)
practices.source: US Army ADP 6-0 Mission Command
practices.what_is_shown: A clear and concise expression of the purpose of the operation and the desired end state, plus key tasks; it sets boundaries for disciplined initiative 'even when the operation does not unfold as planned'. Mission orders state results, not how.
practices.form: Short text paragraph inside an order
practices.decision_types: Delegated execution under uncertainty; downstream decisions made by others without asking back
practices.concrete_example: Subordinates who know purpose, key task and end state act when existing orders no longer fit the situation, then inform superiors of the deviation.
practices.fails_when: Intent too vague to bound action, or so detailed it becomes micromanagement; no shared understanding built through dialogue.

practices.name: Minto Pyramid Principle with SCQ introduction
practices.source: Barbara Minto (ex-McKinsey), The Minto Pyramid Principle
practices.what_is_shown: Ideas organized as a pyramid under a single governing point (answer first), then grouped supporting arguments; introduction uses Situation -> Complication -> Question to identify the question in the reader's mind, which the top point answers.
practices.form: Text structure / slide storyline (action titles in consulting decks)
practices.decision_types: Recommendations to executives, consulting reports, any argument for one answer
practices.concrete_example: Situation: costs stable for years. Complication: a supplier raised prices 18%. Question: should we switch? Answer at top: switch to supplier B in Q2, supported by three grouped reasons.
practices.fails_when: Answer-first framing hides genuinely open options; the pyramid forces a single answer where the decider should choose among value trade-offs; 'power of storytelling' bias (coherent story believed more easily, Lovallo and Sibony).

practices.name: Words of estimative probability (calibrated likelihood words)
practices.source: Sherman Kent, 'Words of Estimative Probability', CIA Studies in Intelligence (declassified)
practices.what_is_shown: Each judgment carries a fixed likelihood term mapped to an odds range (e.g. almost certain, probable, chances about even), so writer and reader mean the same odds.
practices.form: Text convention: likelihood vocabulary table
practices.decision_types: Decisions under uncertainty where the decider acts on forecasts
practices.concrete_example: NIE 29-51 said a Soviet-bloc attack on Yugoslavia in 1951 'should be considered a serious possibility'; Kent meant about 65 to 35, the policy staff read much lower odds, and board members who approved the wording had in mind anywhere from 20 to 80 to 80 to 20.
practices.fails_when: Words used without a shared numeric scale; precise-sounding numbers on unknowable things; readers ignore the scale.

practices.name: Premortem
practices.source: Gary Klein, 'Performing a Project Premortem', Harvard Business Review
practices.what_is_shown: After the plan briefing: 'the project has failed spectacularly'; each person writes reasons independently, then reads one at a time until all are recorded; the owner revises the plan.
practices.form: Facilitated exercise; output is a risk list added to the decision document
practices.decision_types: Before committing to a plan; high-stakes or overconfident teams
practices.concrete_example: In a premortem on air-campaign planning software, a silent team member said one algorithm would take hours on field laptops; developers then revealed a shortcut they had held back, and the project succeeded.
practices.fails_when: Run after the decision is locked; dominated by the senior voice; risks listed but plan not changed.

practices.name: Evidence display over slideware (Challenger and Columbia cases)
practices.source: Edward Tufte, Visual Explanations / Visual and Statistical Thinking (Challenger excerpt); Tufte notebook on Columbia Accident Investigation Board
practices.what_is_shown: Show the one comparison the decision hinges on (cause vs effect across all cases) in a single chart, with uncertainties and assumptions kept next to the conclusion, instead of fragmented bullet slides.
practices.form: Chart (scatter of all cases) and technical paper rather than bullet slides
practices.decision_types: Safety-critical, irreversible go/no-go decisions resting on technical evidence
practices.concrete_example: Thiokol engineers made 13 charts arguing against the cold-weather Challenger launch; none showed O-ring damage against temperature across past flights. CAIB on Columbia: 'the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers' was a problem; the Boeing slide buried that test foam (3 cu in) was far smaller than the actual debris (1920 cu in).
practices.fails_when: Summaries condensed upward drop the uncertainties (CAIB p.201); headings and bullet hierarchy highlight what management already believes; evidence is case-based, not a controlled study.

practices.name: Shopify GSD phase reviews with PM video
practices.source: Glen Coates (VP Product, Shopify) interviewed by Lenny Rachitsky, How Shopify builds product
practices.what_is_shown: Every project goes through five review phases: Proposal, Prototype, Build, Release, Results; reviewers at two levels (directors, then senior leadership) sign off; most reviews include a short PM video: what is this, why valuable, how it works.
practices.form: Internal tool + short video + async comments; sync meeting only for controversial topics
practices.decision_types: Recurring product investment decisions at stage gates; mostly reversible product bets
practices.concrete_example: PM records a short video for the Proposal phase; directors of product, UX, engineering and data comment async; a 30-minute office-hours slot exists for quick feedback.
practices.fails_when: Not stated in source; the interviewee notes very large teams need heavy central coordination. Single company self-report.

practices.name: Segment decisions by type before choosing the format
practices.source: McKinsey Global Survey, Decision making in the age of urgency (Aminov, De Smet, Jost, Mendelsohn)
practices.what_is_shown: Big bets (rare, high stakes): quality of debate - explore alternatives, seek disconfirming information, appoint a devil's advocate. Cross-cutting (frequent, many groups): process and well-run decision meetings. Delegated (frequent, narrow): ownership and speed, little process.
practices.form: Survey-based typology; no document format
practices.decision_types: Meta-level: chooses depth of the decision package
practices.concrete_example: For big bets the three debate practices together made respondents 2.3 times more likely to be 'winners' (43% vs 19%); for delegated decisions empowerment practices 3.9 times (58% vs 15%).
practices.fails_when: Self-reported survey, winners defined by respondents' own ratings; ad hoc decisions not covered.

principles: Triage the decision before choosing the format: reversibility (Bezos Type 1/Type 2) and McKinsey type (big bet / cross-cutting / delegated) decide how heavy the package is. Light process for reversible decisions, full narrative and debate for irreversible ones.

Put the bottom line or the question first (BLUF, Minto, ADR title, DACI 'question?' title, Rust one-paragraph summary). But no serious format stops at one line: the first line routes the reader, and the body carries context, options and consequences.

Always show the alternatives that were rejected and why: Google 'alternatives considered', Rust 'rationale and alternatives' (including 'impact of not doing this'), MADR pros/cons per option, Oxide 'viable options', DACI options table. Completed staff work is the exception, and its weakness is that it hides them.

Make the case against the recommendation explicit: Rust 'Drawbacks', PR/FAQ 'top three reasons this will not succeed' and 'what assumptions need to be true', ADR negative consequences, premortem. McKinsey: for big bets, seeking disconfirming information and a devil's advocate predicted better outcomes.

Show the decision from the user's or customer's seat before the mechanism: PR/FAQ press release and customer quote, Rust guide-level explanation with sample error messages, Shopify PM video. A concrete worked case comes before the technical detail.

Use progressive disclosure by audience: external FAQ before internal FAQ, guide-level before reference-level, overview before details (Google), BLUF before background. Context sits right below the answer and is not hidden behind a click.
Separate objective context (Nygard: 'value-neutral... simply describing facts'; Google: 'objective background facts') from recommendation and judgment.

State uncertainty in calibrated terms (Kent's words of estimative probability, ideally with numbers). Vague phrases like 'serious possibility' were read as anything from 20% to 80% by the people who approved them.

Use a visual only when the decision depends on a relationship or comparison across cases (Challenger temperature vs O-ring damage), or for system context (Google system-context diagram). Bullet-slide summaries condensed up the hierarchy drop the uncertainties (CAIB).
Prose beats bullets for complex reasoning (Amazon six-pager, Nygard: bullets only for visual style). A good memo takes days of rewriting, so the author's effort, not the reader's, carries the load.

Name one decider and the roles around them (DACI single Approver, Netflix informed captain, Uber named approvers). Separate the decision meeting, where dissent is invited, from commitment ('disagree and commit').

Give the decision a lifecycle state and keep superseded decisions (ADR status, Oxide RFD states, MADR 'superseded by'). Add a revisit trigger or confirmation check (MADR Confirmation, Netflix captain reflects after impact is clear).
Log small decisions cheaply where people already read (Stripe Slack decision logs), and give large ones a full document. Both need the why, not only the what.
Process quality around the document matters more than the volume of analysis in it (Lovallo and Sibony: process explained about six times more of decision performance than analysis).
Delegate with intent rather than instructions when others will make the follow-up decisions: purpose, key tasks, end state (commander's intent).
numbers: Amazon memo length: six pages, read silently at the start of the meeting; a high-standards memo 'might take a week or more' (Bezos 2017 letter).
PR/FAQ review: 15-20 minutes silent reading, about 40 minutes discussion; first draft should take a few hours; around 10 contributors for early drafts (workingbackwards.com).
AWS PR/FAQs were written and debated for over a year (2004 to 2006) before S3/EC2 launched (workingbackwards.com).
Bezos 2016: most decisions should be made with about 70% of the information you wish you had.
Google design doc: 10-20 pages for larger projects; 1-3 page mini design doc for incremental work (Ubl 2020).
ADR: one or two pages (Nygard 2011).
Oxide RFD: 3-5 business days for comments before merge as a guideline.
Kent 1964: Board of National Estimates members who agreed on 'serious possibility' meant odds from 20:80 to 80:20; Kent himself meant about 65:35.
Premortem: prospective hindsight increases the ability to correctly identify reasons for future outcomes by 30% (Mitchell, Russo, Pennington 1989, cited by Klein 2007).

Lovallo and Sibony 2010: 1,048 decisions; process mattered more than analysis by a factor of six; moving from bottom to top quartile on process raised ROI by 6.9 percentage points vs 5.3 for analysis (ROI subset n=673).
McKinsey 2019 (n=1,259): only 20% say their organizations excel at decision making; 61% say most decision time is used ineffectively; 37% say decisions are both high quality and fast.

McKinsey 2019: deciding at the right level -> 6.8x more likely to be a 'winner'; big-bet debate practices (alternatives, disconfirming evidence, devil's advocate) -> 2.3x (43% vs 19%); cross-cutting process practices -> 4.5x (45% vs 10%); delegated empowerment -> 3.9x (58% vs 15%).
Challenger: Thiokol prepared 13 charts against the cold launch; none plotted O-ring damage against temperature across prior flights (Tufte 1997).
Columbia: test foam pieces of about 3 cubic inches vs about 1920 cubic inches for the debris that hit the wing, buried in a bullet slide (Tufte / CAIB 2003).
Atlassian DACI page claims '25% higher success rate' from a McKinsey survey; the cited McKinsey PDF contains no such DACI finding (unsupported number).
not_found: No controlled experiment comparing narrative memo vs slides vs one-line summary on decision quality. Tufte's and CAIB's evidence is case-based; a commenter on Tufte's thread asked for such a study and none was cited.
Stripe: no official Stripe decision-document template; only an ex-employee account (Brie Wolfson) and a Pragmatic Engineer piece (not opened).
Shopify: GSD proposal content and template are not public; only interview self-report on phases and PM videos.
McKinsey executive summary / 'action title' guidance: no primary McKinsey style guide found. Only Barbara Minto's site, plus Gene Zelazny's 'Say It With Charts' via secondary pages, not opened.
Bezos 2004 'no PowerPoint' email: not opened; relied on the 2017 shareholder letter instead.

US State Department action memo format (Foreign Affairs Handbook): search returned nothing relevant. The USDA NRCS decision memo with Approve/Disapprove/Discuss was seen only in a search snippet, not opened.
Army FM 6-0 decision paper / staff study format: found in search, not opened.
Uber RFC post date not verified on the fetched page.

Tools: exa was not used (out of credits per task). Firecrawl was rate-limited once and mckinsey.com HTML returned 403, so the McKinsey PDF was read via jina. Serper was used for search. Not checked: Google's internal design doc template, Meta/Microsoft decision docs, Intel/Andy Grove practices, ICD 203 analytic standards.

practices.name: Implementation plan artifact with Proceed button and inline comments (pre-implementation gate)
practices.source: Google Antigravity docs: Implementation plan; Artifacts; Artifact review
practices.what_is_shown: After research, before any file is edited: a Markdown plan of the technical changes needed. It appears as a card in the conversation with a Proceed button. The user can leave Google-Docs-style comments on lines of the plan. Comments collect into a chip ('2 Comments') attached to the next message. The agent then revises the plan and asks again, or starts implementing. A review policy (Always Ask / Always Proceed) decides whether the agent stops; /plan always stops.
practices.form: Rich Markdown document (may include architecture diagrams) plus line-anchored comments plus a single approve button
practices.decision_types: Approach and scope choices before costly or hard-to-reverse work; medium-to-high stakes; tasks the user has not done before. Fast mode skips this gate for small local edits such as renames.
practices.concrete_example: Agent proposes adding a GET /v1/bookmarks endpoint with a new model and router. The user comments 'use the existing pagination helper' and 'drop the caching part'. Then clicks Proceed, and the agent continues with the plan plus those comments.
practices.fails_when: The plan is long relative to the change, so reviewers skim and rubber-stamp it. Under Always Proceed the card may not show a Proceed button, so approval silently becomes a typed 'proceed'. A plan only shows intent; it does not show that the result works.

practices.name: Completion walkthrough with Changes Made + Validation Results + embedded screenshots/recordings
practices.source: Google Antigravity docs: Walkthrough; launch blog 'Introducing Google Antigravity'
practices.what_is_shown: When the task ends, a short summary in a fixed order: what changed, then how it was validated (for example test output: 5 passing tests). For UI work it embeds browser screenshots or recordings with captions. Users can select an area of a screenshot and comment on it.
practices.form: Structured text document with fixed sections, plus images and video, plus comments on the images
practices.decision_types: Accept or iterate after the work is done; async review when the user was not watching live; UI-visible changes
practices.concrete_example: Walkthrough for GET /v1/bookmarks: a 'Changes Made' list of files and endpoints, then 'Validation Results' with npm test output (5 passed). For a homepage task it embeds a screenshot captioned 'Google Antigravity Homepage Hero'.
practices.fails_when: The validation shown is whatever the agent chose to run, and the happy path can pass while edge cases are untested. Screenshots show only static states. Reviewers who never saw the plan lack the 'why'.

practices.name: Task-level progress abstraction instead of tool-call firehose or bare final diff
practices.source: Google Antigravity launch blog (Trust tenet)
practices.what_is_shown: Tool calls are grouped inside tasks. The user sees a task list with high-level progress summaries, and artifacts at milestones: task list, then implementation plan, then walkthrough. Raw tool calls stay inspectable but are not the default view.
practices.form: Hierarchical task list plus milestone artifacts; an inbox and manager view for many parallel agents
practices.decision_types: Supervising several long-running agents asynchronously; deciding when to step in
practices.concrete_example: In Agent Manager, a background research agent shows up in the Inbox with a task-level summary. The user opens its artifact only when notified, not every step.
practices.fails_when: Grouping hides the step where things went wrong, and summaries can paper over a failed sub-step. Google's stated rationale (both extremes erode trust) is design opinion, with no published measurement.

practices.name: Short test plan sent before verification runs
practices.source: Devin docs: Testing & Video Recordings
practices.what_is_shown: Before testing, Devin messages a short plan. It names the single most important end-to-end flow that proves the feature works, as concrete UI steps grounded in the code ('click the button labeled Save at the top right'). Extra flows are added only for a critical edge case. The user can course-correct before execution.
practices.form: Short numbered text message
practices.decision_types: Approving how the work will be proven; cheap, reversible, quick decisions
practices.concrete_example: Test plan: 1) log in as test user; 2) open Settings; 3) toggle dark mode; 4) verify text on the Billing card stays readable. Sent as one chat message, and the user replies 'also check the mobile width'.
practices.fails_when: One flow is chosen and critical paths outside it go unseen. Vague repo testing instructions ('test everything') produce vague plans.

practices.name: Annotated, auto-zoomed screen recording as merge proof
practices.source: Devin docs: Testing & Video Recordings; Computer Use
practices.what_is_shown: After CI is green and review comments are addressed, a short video of the agent using the app. It has text labels at key moments ('Testing login flow', 'Feature confirmed working') and slows down around them. It zooms to where the agent clicks and compresses idle time. It is attached to a chat or Slack message. The stated goal is a reviewer who watches and thinks 'yep, it works', then merges.
practices.form: Processed video with captions, sent as a message attachment
practices.decision_types: Merge decisions for UI-visible features; reviewer does not want to pull the branch; low-to-medium stakes
practices.concrete_example: PR adds CSV export. A 40-second video shows clicking Export, then the file downloading, then the CSV opened with the correct headers, with the caption 'Headers verified'.
practices.fails_when: Devin's own docs say it is a quick sanity check of one primary flow, not exhaustive coverage. It proves the happy path only. Processing can fail (app crash, timeout). It is useless for backend, data or concurrency changes.

practices.name: Merge-ready PR with embedded artifacts (videos, screenshots, logs)
practices.source: Cursor blog 'Cursor agents can now control their own computers'; changelog 02-24-26; Cursor forum bug thread
practices.what_is_shown: The PR description carries artifacts in which the agent demos its own change: a recording of clicking through the feature, screenshots, logs, and a summary of what was tested. Posting to GitHub needs opt-in ('Artifacts' or 'Links').
practices.form: PR description with embedded video, images and logs
practices.decision_types: Merge of UI and feature PRs from autonomous cloud agents; vulnerability reproduction (video of an attack flow)
practices.concrete_example: An agent adds GitHub source links to plugin components. It records itself opening the Prisma plugin and clicking each component to verify the links resolve, and the video goes in the PR.
practices.fails_when: In the forum thread (Feb–Mar 2026), artifacts did not reach GitHub at all, rendered as broken references, or appeared as hallucinated tags. The agent sometimes claimed it recorded a video that never appeared. Artifacts were rewritten only in PR bodies the agent owned, not in comments. A user-side workaround was a comment telling reviewers to 'Open in Web'.

practices.name: PR as a living checklist plus 'View session' logs
practices.source: GitHub blog 'Assigning and completing issues with coding agent in GitHub Copilot'; Microsoft .NET blog 'Ten Months with Copilot Coding Agent in dotnet/runtime'
practices.what_is_shown: The agent opens a draft PR at once. It turns the issue into a checklist in the PR body and ticks items off as it pushes commits. A 'Copilot started work' timeline event links to the session logs, which show what it tried, built and ran. When done it tags the human for review. The issue creator cannot be the final approver.
practices.form: PR body checklist, commit stream, linked step-by-step session log
practices.decision_types: Approve, comment or request changes on well-scoped issues; watching progress or diagnosing why a PR is poor
practices.concrete_example: dotnet/runtime: a reviewer sees an unexpected PR and opens the session log. The log shows the agent trying to build and run tests, which answers 'did it even compile?' that the diff cannot.
practices.fails_when: In May 2025 the agent could not build or test in dotnet/runtime, and the PRs looked confident but were unvalidated: 41.7% success that month, public ridicule on HN and Reddit. Logs are long and few reviewers read them. Volume also overwhelms reviewers: one engineer created 5–9 hours of review work in a few hours (nine PRs at 30–60 min each).

practices.name: Explicit 'what I could not verify' disclosure in the PR description
practices.source: Microsoft .NET blog (CCA instructions); OpenAI 'Introducing Codex'
practices.what_is_shown: The PR description states which paths the agent could not test and asks for human verification. Codex 'explicitly communicates' uncertainty and test failures. In one dotnet case the agent warned against merging in the description, and the PR was closed for exactly that reason.
practices.form: A short caveat section in the text summary
practices.decision_types: Merge decisions where the agent's environment cannot reproduce production (other OS, hardware, credentials); high-stakes repos
practices.concrete_example: 'Could not run the Windows-specific code path in this Linux environment; recommend a human verify on Windows before merge.'
practices.fails_when: The caveat depends on the agent knowing its own blind spots. Without repo instructions that require it, agents rarely volunteer it. A caveat buried at the end of a long description is missed.

practices.name: Claims cited to terminal output and file lines
practices.source: OpenAI 'Introducing Codex' (incl. codex-1 system message)
practices.what_is_shown: The final task summary carries inline citations. File claims point to path and line range (F:path†L10-L20), and test claims point to a terminal-output chunk and line range. The system prompt requires file citations in the Summary section and terminal citations in the Testing section, and keeps citations out of the PR body. Then the user can review, ask for revisions, open a PR, or pull the changes locally.
practices.form: Text summary with clickable evidence anchors into logs and diff
practices.decision_types: Trusting an agent's claims of 'tests pass' or 'changed X' without re-running; async delegation of many parallel tasks
practices.concrete_example: 'Fixed nested CompoundModel separability [F:astropy/modeling/separable.py†L245]. Tests: pytest astropy/modeling passed [chunk_3†L12-L14].'
practices.fails_when: A citation proves a command ran, not that it tested the right thing. Separately, a study of 23,247 agentic PRs found descriptions that claim unimplemented changes to be the most common message-code mismatch (45.4% of high-mismatch cases). Those PRs had 28.3% vs 80.0% acceptance and took 3.5x longer to merge (Gong et al., arXiv 2601.04886).

practices.name: Severity-ranked, verified findings with collapsed 'Why this was flagged' and a non-blocking check
practices.source: Anthropic: 'Bringing Code Review to Claude Code'; Claude Code docs: Code Review, Read and request reviews
practices.date: 2026-03 launch (research preview), later GA; docs read 2026-11-20
practices.what_is_shown: Several agents find candidate bugs, a verification step filters false positives, and the rest are deduplicated and ranked. On the PR: one overview comment, then inline comments on the exact lines with markers (Important 🔴 / Nit 🟡 / Pre-existing 🟣). Reasoning sits in a collapsed 'Why this was flagged' section that explains how the bug was verified. A check-run table sorted by severity has columns Severity, File:Line, Issue. A machine-readable line gives counts per severity for CI gating. The review never approves or blocks; the merge stays human. Later reviews say how many nits or out-of-scope findings were 'found and not posted'.
practices.form: Summary comment, inline comments, severity table, expandable rationale, JSON severity counts
practices.decision_types: Merge decisions on any PR size; especially routine-looking small diffs with hidden blast radius; teams wanting CI gates on 'Important > 0'
practices.concrete_example: A one-line production change is flagged 🔴 Important: 'would break authentication for the service'. Expanding 'Why this was flagged' shows the traced call path. The author fixes it before merge.
practices.fails_when: No findings does not mean safe (docs say so explicitly). It costs $15–25 per review and takes about 20 minutes. Replies do not dismiss findings, so threads must be resolved. Severity labels compress context, and a Nit on one PR can be critical on another.

practices.name: Logically ordered diff walkthrough with per-hunk explanation and colored flags
practices.source: Cognition blog 'Devin Review: AI to Stop Slop'
practices.what_is_shown: Instead of GitHub's alphabetical file order, changes are grouped by logical connection and ordered so the reviewer reads top to bottom. Each hunk carries an explanation, like a colleague walking you through the PR. Moved or copied code is detected and not shown as delete-plus-add. Bug flags are coloured red (probable bug), yellow (warning) and gray (FYI). Inline chat answers questions about code outside the diff.
practices.form: Reordered, annotated diff (a case narrated in sequence) plus colored issue list plus inline Q&A
practices.decision_types: Large PRs where reviewers would otherwise give a 'Lazy LGTM'; agent-authored PRs past the reviewer's ability to hold in their head
practices.concrete_example: A PR touching schema, migration, API and UI is shown as: 1) schema change and why; 2) migration that backfills it; 3) API using the new field; 4) UI. A red flag sits on the migration's null handling.
practices.fails_when: The agent's narrative can steer the reviewer toward its own framing. HN commenters report juniors trusting AI-highlighted hotspots and leaving other parts unreviewed. The grouping can be wrong for cross-cutting changes.

practices.name: Walkthrough comment: grouped change table, sequence diagram, effort score, merge risk, linked-issue gap
practices.source: CodeRabbit docs: PR Walkthroughs
practices.what_is_shown: Optional summary at top. A changed-files table that groups related files into rows with plain-language descriptions (one source file plus 27 locale files gives 2 rows). A Mermaid sequence diagram of the new flow when components interact. Estimated review effort 1–5. Merge Risk from Minimal to Critical, with an explanation and the commit it covers. Linked-issue assessment showing gaps between what the issue asked and what the PR delivers. Related issues and PRs, suggested labels and reviewers. Collapsed by default; each section can be toggled.
practices.form: Table plus diagram plus scores plus collapsible details
practices.decision_types: Triage (which PR to review first); understanding flow changes in APIs and async workflows; checking scope against the ticket
practices.concrete_example: PR adds async webhook retries. The walkthrough shows a sequence diagram Client -> API -> Queue -> Worker -> Webhook with the retry loop, Effort 3/5, Merge Risk Medium ('retry has no backoff cap'), and Linked issue #123: 'idempotency key requirement not addressed'.
practices.fails_when: Users on HN and Reddit (2024–2025) complain of noise: too many low-value comments, nitpicks despite instructions, comments on code already removed. The extras (poem, ASCII art, fortunes) erode seriousness. Diagrams are generated only when a flow exists and can misstate the flow.

practices.name: Plan approval prompt with autonomy choice and editable plan
practices.source: Claude Code docs: Permission modes (plan mode)
practices.what_is_shown: After read-only research Claude presents the plan and asks how to proceed. The options combine approval with how much autonomy follows: 'Yes, and use auto mode' / 'Yes, manually approve edits' / 'No, keep planning' (free-text feedback). Ctrl+G opens the plan in the user's editor to change it directly. An optional first option approves and clears the planning context.
practices.form: Plan document plus a 3–4 option menu plus a free-text alternative
practices.decision_types: Approach approval before edits; choosing how closely to supervise the execution phase
practices.concrete_example: Plan: 'Add bulk insert for EOD prices: 1) batch rows in chunks of 1,000; 2) replace per-row INSERT in repository; 3) add test.' The user presses Ctrl+G, deletes step 3's new test framework, then picks 'Yes, manually approve edits'.
practices.fails_when: In issue #12366 (Nov 2025), after v2.0.51 plans grew to 300–800+ lines for about 50-line changes. Users pinned old versions, said the plan took longer to read than the code, and in the terminal could not see the plan contents ('Am I supposed to trust the summary?'). The reporter later concluded plans are 'material to ASK agents about, not to review as a Human'.

practices.name: Spec Mode: read-only spec, then approve-with-autonomy-level, saved as dated Markdown
practices.source: Factory docs: Interaction Modes (Spec Mode)
practices.what_is_shown: Droid researches read-only and proposes a concrete implementation plan, then asks for approval. The options are: proceed with manual approvals, proceed at Low, Medium or High autonomy, or keep iterating on the spec. Organization policy can hide the higher options. An approved spec can be auto-saved as YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md in .factory/docs.
practices.form: Spec document plus an approval menu that sets the execution autonomy level; persisted Markdown
practices.decision_types: Architecture changes, migrations, security-sensitive work; decisions that should be auditable later
practices.concrete_example: Spec for password reset: email token, 24-hour expiry, rate limiting, tests for expired and invalid links, following the report-generation background-job pattern. The user approves with 'Auto (Low)', and the spec is saved as .factory/docs/2026-11-20-password-reset.md.
practices.fails_when: The spec's quality depends on the request stating outcome, constraints and verification. Approval with High autonomy turns one decision into many unreviewed actions. No published data on how often specs are actually read.

practices.name: Agent session states + typed activities + select-option elicitations + live plan checklist
practices.source: Linear Developers: Agent Interaction, Signals, Agent Interaction Guidelines (AIG)
practices.what_is_shown: Each agent run is a session with a visible state: pending, active, awaitingInput, error, complete, stale. The agent must acknowledge within 10 seconds. It emits typed activities: thought, action (with parameter and result), elicitation (question), response (final), error. An elicitation with the 'select' signal renders options, but the user may ignore them and reply in free text. A session-level plan checklist (pending, inProgress, completed, canceled) is replaced whole on each update. The PR link sits in the session's external URLs. AIG principles: disclose being an agent, show internal state at a glance with reasoning inspectable on demand, respect 'stop', and the human remains accountable.
practices.form: Status chip plus activity timeline plus option buttons plus checklist inside the issue
practices.decision_types: Small clarifying choices mid-task (which repo or package); delegation status; stop or continue
practices.concrete_example: Elicitation 'Which package in the monorepo are you referring to?' with buttons frontend / backend. The user instead types 'neither, it's the shared utils', which is accepted as a prompt.
practices.fails_when: Built for short choices, not for big decisions needing context. Free-text answers require an LLM to interpret them. Ephemeral thought and action items vanish, so the trail for later audit is thin.

practices.name: Approval request for a specific function call, routed to Slack or email, with approve / deny-with-reason
practices.source: HumanLayer SDK (npm @humanlayer/sdk); 12-factor-agents Factor 7
practices.date: 2025 (12-factor agents published 2025; SDK page 'published a year ago')
practices.what_is_shown: Sensitive functions are wrapped with requireApproval. The human gets the exact call the agent wants to make (function plus arguments) in a configured channel, with context about who the approver is. Response options carry a name, title, description and a prefilled feedback prompt ('Denied because...'). A denial plus its reason goes back into the agent's context. The structured human-contact request has the form {question, context, options: {urgency low|medium|high, format free_text|yes_no|multiple_choice, choices}}.
practices.form: Chat message with buttons plus a free-text rejection reason; agent pauses durably until the webhook reply
practices.decision_types: Single irreversible side effects (send email, deploy to production, payments); outer-loop agents started by cron or events, where nobody is watching a chat
practices.concrete_example: 'Would you like to proceed with deploying v1.2.3 to production?' Context: 'production deployment affecting live users'; urgency high; yes/no. The reply 'can you deploy the backend first?' is fed back as a rejection with feedback.
practices.fails_when: The approver sees raw arguments without the surrounding reasoning or diff, so judging blast radius is hard. High-frequency asks become reflexive approvals. No timeout or escalation by default unless configured.

practices.name: Route only risky actions to a human; auto-approve the rest; escalate after repeated denials
practices.source: Anthropic Engineering: 'How we built Claude Code auto mode'
practices.what_is_shown: Instead of a prompt per action (users accept 93% of them, which signals approval fatigue), a classifier judges each risky action against user intent. Reads and in-project edits pass without a prompt. A blocked action returns to the agent with a reason so it can find a safer path. The human is asked only after 3 consecutive or 20 total denials.
practices.form: Policy and routing mechanism; the human sees far fewer, higher-stakes prompts
practices.decision_types: High-volume low-stakes actions vs rare irreversible ones (force-push, prod deploy, credential use, data exfiltration)
practices.concrete_example: The user says 'clean up old branches'. The agent tries to batch-delete remote branches. This is blocked as scope escalation, because a vague request does not authorize an irreversible remote delete.
practices.fails_when: 17% false-negative rate on real overeager actions. The classifier finds 'approval-shaped evidence' (an earlier similar approval, a vague 'clean up the PR') and treats it as consent for a larger blast radius. Anthropic says it is not a replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure.

principles: Show work at the task level, not as a stream of every tool call and not as a bare final diff. Antigravity's stated design goal is the 'necessary and sufficient set of artifacts and verification results'.

Use two gates: approve intent before costly work (plan or spec), then accept the outcome with evidence after (walkthrough, video, cited tests). Products that skip the first gate default to 'fast mode' for small local edits only.

Evidence beats narrative. Tie every claim to an artifact the reviewer can check: terminal-output citations (Codex), a test-run section (Antigravity), video of the feature working (Devin, Cursor). Descriptions that claim things the code does not do cut acceptance from 80.0% to 28.3%.
State what was NOT verified, explicitly and up front, such as an untested OS path or a missing credential. It changes reviewer behaviour and once caused a correct 'do not merge'.

Rank by severity, verify before showing, and hide reasoning behind an expander. Anthropic Code Review shows Important / Nit / Pre-existing markers, a collapsed 'Why this was flagged', and counts of findings it chose not to post.

Order a large change as a narrated case, not alphabetically. Group related hunks, explain each, and collapse moves and renames (Devin Review). Use a sequence diagram only when the change alters a flow between components (CodeRabbit).
Keep length proportional to the change. 800-line plans for about 50-line changes made users pin old versions, and long plans stop being read and become 'material to ask the agent about'.
Offer options plus an escape hatch. Approval menus combine 'yes' with the autonomy level for the next phase (Claude Code, Factory), and option buttons never block a free-text answer (Linear select).
Attach feedback to the artifact instead of restarting. Inline comments on plans and select-and-comment on screenshots are carried into the agent's next step without stopping it (Antigravity).
Too-frequent asks turn into rubber stamps (93% of permission prompts accepted). Route only irreversible or out-of-scope actions to the human and auto-handle the rest.

Video proves one happy path for UI-visible changes: one primary flow, annotated, idle time cut. It is explicitly not a substitute for test coverage, and it fails silently when artifacts do not attach.
The agent never approves; the human stays accountable (Linear AIG; Code Review never approves or blocks; the issue creator cannot be the final approver of a Copilot PR).
Give a machine-readable verdict next to the human-readable one, so mechanical gates (such as 'Important findings > 0 fails CI') do not depend on a person reading prose.
Reviewer capacity, not generation, is the bottleneck. Every format should be judged by minutes-to-confident-decision. One engineer created 5–9 hours of review work in a few hours of delegation.
numbers: Anthropic Code Review: PRs with substantive review comments rose from 16% to 54% at Anthropic; on 1,000+ line PRs 84% get findings (avg 7.5); on <50-line PRs 31% (avg 0.5); <1% of findings marked incorrect; avg review ~20 min; $15–25 per review (claude.com/resources/articles/code-review)

Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts; auto-mode classifier: 0.4% FPR on 10,000 real actions, 17% FNR on 52 real overeager actions; escalates to the human after 3 consecutive or 20 total denials (anthropic.com/research/claude-code-auto-mode)

PR message-code inconsistency: 406 of 23,247 agentic PRs (1.7%) high-MCI; 'claims unimplemented changes' = 45.4% of those; acceptance 28.3% vs 80.0%; merge time 55.8 vs 16.0 hours (arXiv 2601.04886, MSR'26)

dotnet/runtime Copilot coding agent: 878 PRs, 535 merged, 67.9% success vs 87.1% for Microsoft humans; 41.7% in May 2025 when it could not build or test; 38.1% before vs 69% after environment setup changes; revert rate 0.6% vs 0.8% for non-agent PRs; 1–50 line PRs succeed 76–80%, 101–500 lines 64% (devblogs.microsoft.com, 2026-03)
dotnet/runtime: 9 complex agent PRs opened in a few hours created 5–9 hours of review work (30–60 min each); 7 of 9 merged

Agentic PR outcomes: of 9,799 human-reviewed closed agentic PRs, only 35.7% of rejections reflected clear agent failure; 31.2% were workflow constraints; 33.1% had no observable rationale; 15.4% of merged PRs needed explicit reviewer feedback or commits (arXiv 2605.22534, MSR 2026)
Security-related agentic PRs: rejection is more strongly associated with PR complexity and verbosity than with security topic (arXiv 2601.00477)
Cursor: over 30% of PRs merged at Cursor are created by autonomous cloud agents (cursor.com/blog/agent-computer-use, 2026-02-24)
Claude Code plan mode regression report: 300–800+ line plans for ~50-line code changes after v2.0.51 (github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/12366)
not_found: No vendor published a controlled measurement of which presentation format (video vs text vs diagram vs cited summary) improves approval accuracy or review time. The format claims above are design statements or practice, not A/B results.
Linear: I found the agent session and activity API and the AIG principles, but not agent-written project or initiative 'updates' as a feature. I did not search Linear's changelog for such updates.
Factory: I found only Spec Mode approval. No dedicated 'report' artifact turned up. Missions/Mission Control validation milestones were mentioned but not read.
HumanLayer: I saw the SDK and 12-factor patterns only. I did not see a screenshot or spec of the actual Slack approval message layout, and the current CodeLayer product was not checked.
OpenAI Codex: only the May 2025 launch post was read, and OpenAI marks it outdated. The current 2026 Codex task summary and PR UI was not checked.
GitHub Copilot: the official docs page on the PR description format was not read; the claims come from the GitHub blog and the .NET retrospective.
Antigravity: no user complaints or praise were searched for, only first-party docs.
Cursor: the Cloud Agents docs page on artifact settings and the Bugbot review format were not read.
All search went through fetchira with the serper provider; Exa was not used (out of credits). Several docs pages were undated, and their dates are given as the 2026-11-20 read date.

practices.name: Human-first, then AI (update / provisional-decision workflow)
practices.source: Bucinca, Malaya, Gajos, 'To Trust or to Think', CSCW 2021; Fogliato et al., 'Who Goes First?', FAccT 2022
practices.what_is_shown: 1) The case and raw facts only. 2) The decider records a provisional answer. 3) Only then the AI recommendation plus explanation is revealed. 4) Decider may update.
practices.form: Two-step interactive flow (form field or button before reveal)
practices.decision_types: Familiar, moderately high-stakes decisions where the decider has real domain knowledge; not for time-critical ones. Best when the cost of a wrong AI-accepted answer is high.
practices.concrete_example: Pipeline asks 'Merge strategy for this repo: squash or merge commits? Your pick:' and only after the owner taps one shows 'Agent recommends squash because ...' with an 'I changed my mind' option.
practices.fails_when: Decider has no independent basis (unfamiliar domain): the forced guess is noise. Users dislike it (lowest subjective ratings in Bucinca N=199). In Fogliato (19 radiologists) it lowered agreement with the AI whether the AI was right or wrong, and reduced seeking a colleague's second opinion; benefits accrue mostly to people high in Need for Cognition.

practices.name: On-demand recommendation (AI answer hidden until requested)
practices.source: Bucinca, Malaya, Gajos, CSCW 2021
practices.what_is_shown: The case first; a 'See AI's suggestion' button reveals recommendation + explanation only on click.
practices.form: Interactive disclosure (collapsed recommendation)
practices.decision_types: Routine-to-moderate stakes, decider is competent; reversible decisions where you want the human to think first but not be blocked.
practices.concrete_example: Decision card shows the question and the three options with their facts; the line 'Agent's pick' is collapsed behind 'Show recommendation'.
practices.fails_when: Low-motivation deciders click immediately, collapsing it back into plain recommendation. Cognitive forcing designs as a group reduced overreliance on wrong AI vs simple XAI but no condition beat the no-AI baseline when the AI was wrong.

practices.name: Explanation without recommendation (evidence only, human concludes)
practices.source: Gajos & Mamykina, 'Do People Engage Cognitively with AI?', IUI 2022
practices.what_is_shown: Relevant facts and reasoning about each option (the explanation), but no verdict; the human must derive the decision.
practices.form: Text structure: per-option facts and trade-offs, no 'recommended' badge
practices.decision_types: Recurring decision types where you want the owner to build skill and stay calibrated; medium stakes; not urgent.
practices.concrete_example: 'Option A: 2 days, touches 3 services, rollback = revert. Option B: 5 days, one service, no rollback.' and no line saying which to pick.
practices.fails_when: Time pressure or many small decisions: it costs effort per decision. In experiments 1-2 (recommendation+explanation, before or after own choice) decisions improved but no learning; only explanation-only produced both better decisions and learning.

practices.name: Contrastive explanation against the human's likely choice
practices.source: Bucinca, Swaroop, Paluch, Doshi-Velez, Gajos, CHI 2025
practices.what_is_shown: The AI's choice, the predicted human choice, and specifically why they differ ('why A rather than the B you would likely pick').
practices.form: Short text block 'Why not X' next to the recommendation
practices.decision_types: Recurring decisions where the system can model the decider's default; skill-building matters; medium stakes.
practices.concrete_example: 'You usually pick the faster option. Here the faster option (B) skips the migration test, and the last two times that broke staging.'
practices.fails_when: Predicted human choice is wrong, so the contrast addresses a misconception the user does not have. N=628: improved independent decision skill vs unilateral explanations without loss of accuracy; effect on one-shot novel decisions untested.

practices.name: Two-sided (pro and con) explanation instead of one-sided justification
practices.source: Si et al., 'LLMs Help Humans Verify Truthfulness - Except When They Are Convincingly Wrong', NAACL 2024
practices.what_is_shown: The strongest case for and the strongest case against the claim or option, side by side, before or alongside any verdict.
practices.form: Two-column text (for / against) or steelman + critique
practices.decision_types: Verification-type decisions (is this claim/plan correct?), high stakes, where the LLM can be fluently wrong.
practices.concrete_example: 'Why merging now is right: ... / Why merging now is wrong: ...' with links to the diff and test results.
practices.fails_when: Both sides written by the same model share its blind spot. In the study (80 crowdworkers) contrastive explanations reduced overreliance vs one-sided LLM explanations but did not significantly beat reading search results; showing LLM text plus retrieved passages gave no complementary benefit over passages alone.

practices.name: Questions instead of statements (AI-framed questioning)
practices.source: Danry, Pataranutaporn, Mao, Maes, CHI 2023
practices.what_is_shown: Instead of 'X is wrong because Y', the AI asks the decider a question that points at Y ('Does the premise actually support the conclusion?').
practices.form: Text: 1-3 targeted questions
practices.decision_types: Judgment and critical-review decisions (is this argument/plan sound?), low time pressure.
practices.concrete_example: 'Before approving: what happens to in-flight jobs if this deploy is rolled back?' rather than 'Rollback will drop in-flight jobs.'
practices.fails_when: Decider needs a fast answer or lacks knowledge to answer the question. N=204: improved discernment of flawed statements vs no feedback and vs causal explanations from an always-correct AI; tested on logic validity, not on operational decisions.

practices.name: Calibrated confidence display (per-case)
practices.source: Zhang, Liao, Bellamy, FAT* 2020; Ma et al., CHI 2023
practices.what_is_shown: Recommendation plus a per-case confidence (and, in Ma et al., an estimate of the human's own likely correctness on similar cases).
practices.form: Number or band next to recommendation; optionally 'you vs AI' correctness likelihood
practices.decision_types: Recurring decisions with a track record from which confidence can be calibrated.
practices.concrete_example: 'Recommend: retry the job. Confidence: low (in 14 similar cases the agent was right 6 times). Your record on similar cases: 11/14.'
practices.fails_when: Confidence is not calibrated (typical of verbalized LLM confidence). Zhang: confidence calibrated trust but did not improve joint accuracy when humans had no complementary knowledge; local feature explanations did not help. Ma et al. (N=293): adding human correctness likelihood promoted more appropriate trust than AI confidence alone.

practices.name: First-person hedged uncertainty in LLM text
practices.source: Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard, Vaughan, FAccT 2024
practices.what_is_shown: The recommendation phrased with an explicit first-person uncertainty marker when the system is unsure ('I'm not sure, but ...').
practices.form: Natural-language wording
practices.decision_types: Any LLM-generated recommendation where the model's reliability varies case to case.
practices.concrete_example: 'I'm not sure, but I think the flaky test is caused by the timezone fixture.'
practices.fails_when: Used uniformly regardless of actual confidence (becomes noise and erodes trust where the AI is right). N=404 pre-registered: first-person uncertainty reduced agreement and increased accuracy, reducing but not eliminating overreliance; general-perspective phrasing ('It's not clear') had weaker, non-significant effects.

practices.name: Length control: explanation length matched to confidence
practices.source: Steyvers et al., 'What large language models know and what people think they know', Nature Machine Intelligence 2025
practices.what_is_shown: Explanation whose length and tone are adjusted to reflect the model's internal confidence; no padding.
practices.form: Text length and wording policy
practices.decision_types: All LLM-presented recommendations.
practices.concrete_example: A low-confidence recommendation gets two sentences with an explicit 'uncertain'; a high-confidence one gets the same length, not more.
practices.fails_when: Longer, more detailed explanations raise user confidence even when they add no accuracy; default LLM explanations led users to overestimate accuracy. Aligning wording to internal confidence narrowed both calibration and discrimination gaps.

practices.name: Example-based / case-based evidence (similar past cases)
practices.source: Cai et al., 'Human-Centered Tools for Coping with Imperfect Algorithms', CHI 2019 (SMILY); Cai, Jongejan, Holbrook, IUI 2019; van der Waa et al., Artificial Intelligence 2021
practices.what_is_shown: Past cases similar to the current one, with what was decided and how it turned out; ideally one case on each side of the decision boundary (contrastive examples) and tools to refine what 'similar' means.
practices.form: Case gallery or short case cards; interactive refine-by-attribute
practices.decision_types: Recurring decisions with an archive of outcomes; expert deciders; pattern-matching domains.
practices.concrete_example: 'Similar: 2026-09 schema migration on service X, chose staged rollout, 0 incidents. Counter-case: 2026-07 same choice on service Y, 2h outage because of lock contention.'
practices.fails_when: Retrieval similarity differs from the decider's notion of relevance (SMILY needed refinement tools). Normative examples raised perceived understanding while comparative examples sometimes lowered perceived capability by exposing limits (QuickDraw, 1150 users). van der Waa (insulin dosing) found neither rule-based nor example-based contrastive explanations improved task performance; rule-based gave only small gains in understanding.

practices.name: Frequency-based uncertainty graphics (quantile dotplots, icon arrays)
practices.source: Fernandes, Walls, Munson, Hullman, Kay, CHI 2018; Galesic, Garcia-Retamero, Gigerenzer, Health Psychology 2009
practices.what_is_shown: Outcome distribution as countable discrete outcomes (e.g. 20 or 50 dots, 100 icons) instead of a point estimate or a text interval.
practices.form: Chart: quantile dotplot, CDF plot, or icon array
practices.decision_types: Decisions under quantified uncertainty: timing, risk, duration estimates, cost ranges; repeated decisions.
practices.concrete_example: Estimated task duration shown as 20 dots: 12 dots land within 2 days, 6 within 3-5 days, 2 beyond a week, instead of 'about 2 days'.
practices.fails_when: No real distribution exists (fake precision), or one-off qualitative choices. Fernandes: 50-dot quantile dotplots gave expected payoff 97% of optimal, 5 pp above no-uncertainty control (95% CI 2-8) and 4 pp less within-subject variability; CDFs nearly as good; textual intervals were sensitive to the interval chosen. Icon arrays mainly help low-numeracy readers.

practices.name: Mediating Assessments Protocol (score dimensions before the holistic verdict)
practices.source: Kahneman, Lovallo, Sibony, MIT Sloan Management Review 2019
practices.what_is_shown: A predefined short list of criteria; each scored independently from its own evidence; make-or-break criteria first; the full profile of scores displayed; only then the overall narrative and decision.
practices.form: Table / scorecard per criterion, then holistic judgment
practices.decision_types: High-stakes, hard-to-reverse, multi-attribute decisions (strategic, hiring, architecture); also recurrent decisions for learning.
practices.concrete_example: Architecture choice card: Reversibility 2/5, Cost 4/5, Operational risk 3/5, Fit with existing stack 5/5, each with its evidence line; recommendation narrative appears only below the profile.
practices.fails_when: Criteria are chosen after seeing options (rationalization), or scores are copied from the overall impression (halo). Evidence for strategy is anecdotal (authors: 'quantitative effects will take years'); the measured basis is the structured-interview literature.

practices.name: Reversibility triage (one-way vs two-way doors)
practices.source: Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2015 shareholder letter (SEC exhibit)
practices.what_is_shown: First, whether the decision is reversible and at what cost; then the depth of process: light for two-way doors, heavy for one-way doors.
practices.form: Label/classification on the decision card that controls how much is shown
practices.decision_types: Routing rule for all decisions: sets which presentation format to use.
practices.concrete_example: Card header 'Reversible: yes, revert in 5 min' leads to a compact card; 'Irreversible: deletes production data' leads to the full MAP scorecard plus pre-mortem.
practices.fails_when: Reversibility is misjudged (hidden coupling, data loss, reputational effects). Bezos warns large organizations tend to apply the heavyweight process everywhere; no outcome measurement published.

practices.name: Pre-mortem section
practices.source: Gary Klein, 'Performing a Project Premortem', HBR 2007
practices.what_is_shown: Assume the chosen option has failed in N months; list the most plausible reasons; shown after the recommendation.
practices.form: Short bulleted list under the recommendation
practices.decision_types: High-stakes, plan-like decisions with execution risk; teams prone to groupthink.
practices.concrete_example: 'It is March and the migration failed. Most likely because: 1) lock contention on the orders table, 2) the backfill exceeded the maintenance window.'
practices.fails_when: Becomes a boilerplate list generated by the same LLM that wrote the plan; Klein cites prospective-hindsight research (Mitchell, Russo, Pennington 1989) but the premortem itself lacks controlled outcome studies (not verified).

practices.name: Narrative memo read before discussion
practices.source: Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2017 shareholder letter
practices.what_is_shown: A narratively structured document (up to six pages) stating the problem, context, options and reasoning, read silently by all before the decision meeting.
practices.form: Long-form text document
practices.decision_types: Large, novel, cross-cutting decisions where reasoning quality matters more than speed.
practices.concrete_example: A 2-page decision memo for 'Which tracker for the agent pipeline' with context, options, trade-offs, recommendation, open risks; read before answering.
practices.fails_when: Small or frequent decisions (overhead); writing quality varies widely; Bezos notes great memos take a week or more. No controlled evidence of better decisions.

practices.name: Deliberation dialogue on disagreement (dimension-level)
practices.source: Ma et al., 'Towards Human-AI Deliberation', CHI 2025
practices.what_is_shown: Human states their view per dimension; AI shows where it disagrees per dimension, with evidence; they discuss conflicting dimensions; decision updated.
practices.form: Interactive conversation scoped to conflicting dimensions
practices.decision_types: Multi-criteria decisions where the human and AI may weigh factors differently; enough time for dialogue.
practices.concrete_example: Owner rates 'risk' as low; agent shows the two dimensions where it disagrees (rollback cost, test coverage) and the evidence for each; owner can ask follow-ups.
practices.fails_when: Exploratory evaluation on graduate admissions only; time-costly; LLM can talk the human into its view (persuasion rather than evidence).

practices.name: Choice set size and default option
practices.source: Chernev, Bockenholt, Goodman, J. Consumer Psychology 2015; Jachimowicz et al., Behavioural Public Policy 2019
practices.what_is_shown: A small number of options (2-4) with one pre-selected default (the recommendation).
practices.form: Buttons/options with one primary
practices.decision_types: Frequent, low-stakes, reversible decisions; deciders with low preference certainty.
practices.concrete_example: Two buttons: 'Squash (recommended)' as primary and 'Keep commits' as secondary.
practices.fails_when: Defaults increase uptake of the pre-selected option by d = 0.68 (95% CI 0.53-0.83) across 58 studies, so a wrong default propagates errors; that is the overreliance mechanism. Choice overload has no reliable main effect; it appears with complex sets, hard tasks, uncertain preferences and effort-minimizing goals (99 observations, N=7202). Hiding real alternatives to cut options is a failure mode.

practices.name: Progressive disclosure (summary first, detail on demand)
practices.source: Nielsen Norman Group, 'Progressive Disclosure'
practices.what_is_shown: Primary layer: the few items needed for most decisions; secondary layer: rarely needed detail behind an explicit control.
practices.form: Collapsible sections, drawers, 'more' links
practices.decision_types: Decisions where most readers need the same few facts and only some need depth; works for low-stakes; risky for high-stakes if the key risk is hidden.
practices.concrete_example: Card: question, options, recommendation and the single biggest risk visible; context, logs and cases collapsed.
practices.fails_when: The split between primary and secondary is wrong: decisive information (e.g., the irreversibility or the counter-evidence) gets hidden, and combined with a default it yields rubber-stamping. Nielsen's guidance is about feature complexity, not tested on AI decision quality.

principles: Explanations alone do not fix overreliance: in Bansal et al. (CHI 2021) explanations increased acceptance of AI advice regardless of correctness; the Schemmer et al. meta-analysis (AIES 2022) found no effect of explanations over bare AI predictions.

Human+AI is on average worse than the better of the two alone (Hedges g = -0.23, 95% CI -0.39 to -0.07; Vaccaro et al. 2024) but better than humans alone (g = 0.64); losses concentrate in decision tasks, and gains appear when the human is better than the AI. Confidence displays and explanations did not significantly moderate this.

Sequence matters more than content: showing the AI verdict first anchors; making the human commit or think first (update, on-demand, wait, explanation-only) reduces overreliance, and the cost is effort and lower satisfaction.

People engage with an explanation only when that is cheaper than trusting the AI (Vasconcelos et al. 2023, 5 studies, N=731): explanations must make verifying cheaper, for example by linking to the evidence or a diff, not by adding prose.

Longer explanations raise confidence without raising accuracy (Steyvers et al. 2025): length should follow the evidence, and uncertainty should be stated in the first person when present (Kim et al. 2024).
Prefer contrast over justification: pro/con, 'why not your likely choice', and counter-example cases beat one-sided rationales.

Match depth to the decision type: reversible and frequent decisions get a compact card with a default; irreversible, high-stakes or novel decisions get structured per-criterion assessment, pre-mortem and evidence before the verdict.
A strong default (d around 0.68) is a powerful lever, so only set one when the recommender is reliable for that decision class; otherwise it amplifies errors.
Show uncertainty as frequencies or distributions where numbers exist; text intervals are fragile.

Cognitive forcing benefits motivated, high-Need-for-Cognition deciders more; design for the decider's actual effort budget and track reliance outcomes, not satisfaction (Bucinca et al. 2020 showed that subjective measures can mislead).
numbers: Default effects meta-analysis: d = 0.68 (95% CI 0.53-0.83), 58 studies (Jachimowicz et al. 2019).

Choice overload meta-analysis: 99 observations, N = 7202; there is no main effect without moderators; complexity, task difficulty, preference uncertainty and effort-minimizing goal drive overload (Chernev et al. 2015).

Nudge meta-analysis d = 0.43 (95% CI 0.38-0.48) (Mertens et al., PNAS 2022); Maier et al. (PNAS 2022) found no evidence of an average effect after publication-bias correction (category-level detail not checked).
Human-AI vs best of either alone: g = -0.23 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.07); vs human alone: g = 0.64 (95% CI 0.53-0.74); more than 100 studies and more than 300 effect sizes (Vaccaro et al. 2024).
Quantile dotplot (50 dots): 97% of optimal payoff (95% CI 95-98%), +5 pp over control (95% CI 2-8), within-subject SD 4 pp lower (Fernandes et al. 2018).
Showing AI predicted labels: more than 20% relative improvement in human accuracy on deception detection; explanations alone improved it only slightly (Lai & Tan 2019).

Sample sizes: Bucinca 2021 N = 199; Vasconcelos 2023 N = 731; Kim 2024 N = 404; Bucinca 2025 N = 628; Ma 2023 N = 293; Danry 2023 N = 204; Si 2024 N = 80; Fogliato 2022 N = 19 radiologists; Cai 2019 QuickDraw 1150 users.

Lovallo & Sibony (McKinsey 2010): in 1,048 business decisions, process mattered more than analysis by a factor of six (survey-based; the primary page was blocked, so this comes from the search snippet and a mirror).
