not_found: Exact overreliance percentages per condition in Bucinca et al. 2021: the tables did not survive text extraction, so the effect is reported qualitatively only.
Any controlled study of the Amazon memo, premortem, or the Mediating Assessments Protocol on decision outcomes: these are practice or opinion only.
Measured studies of video or diagram formats for presenting AI recommendations to a decider: none found in this pass (searched only through the sources above).

Studies of decision presentation specifically for owner-to-agent-pipeline approvals (software agents asking a human to approve): none found; the closest are the LLM studies (Kim 2024, Si 2024, Steyvers 2025, Ma 2025).
Studies of Jacobs et al. 2021 (clinicians) and of Swaroop et al. on time pressure: not checked in this pass.
Effect sizes for progressive disclosure on decision quality: none found; the NN/g guidance is about usability.
Search note: all searches used fetchira with provider serper; mckinsey.com returned 403 and PubMed required cookies, so those two were not read directly.

practices.name: Cognitive fit: choose table or graph by the task, not by taste
practices.source: Iris Vessey, 'Cognitive Fit: A Theory-Based Analysis of the Graphs Versus Tables Literature', Decision Sciences 22(2), 1991; Vessey & Galletta, ISR 1991
practices.what_is_shown: First decide the task type. Spatial tasks (see a trend, a relationship, a comparison of shapes) get a graph. Symbolic tasks (read an exact value, look up a number) get a table. Representation and task are matched before anything is drawn.
practices.form: Table or chart, picked by a rule
practices.decision_types: Any decision that rests on numbers. It matters most for familiar, repeated decisions where the same task comes up again and again.
practices.concrete_example: 'Is the agent pipeline getting slower week over week?' is a spatial question, so show a line chart. 'Exactly how many tokens did yesterday's run cost?' is a symbolic question, so show a table cell.
practices.fails_when: The decision mixes both kinds of task, or the reader prefers tables even when graphs fit better. Vessey & Galletta saw subjects prefer tables and symbolic problems. Only the abstract was read; the full text sits behind a bot wall.

practices.name: Task complexity changes the table-vs-graph result
practices.source: Cheri Speier, 'The influence of information presentation formats on complex task decision-making performance', International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 64(11), 2006
practices.what_is_shown: Same rule as cognitive fit, extended to complex tasks. Spatial formats (graphs) gave better accuracy on simple and complex spatial tasks, and faster decisions on every task except complex symbolic ones, where graphs and tables took the same time.
practices.form: Lab experiment that compared graph and table formats
practices.decision_types: Complex multi-criteria business decisions such as production planning
practices.concrete_example: For a decision about where cost spikes cluster across 12 repos and 8 weeks, a graph wins. For a decision that needs exact budget arithmetic across many cells, a table does just as well.
practices.fails_when: Graphs bring no speed advantage on complex symbolic tasks. Spatial ability also moderates the effect, so a reader with weak spatial skills gains less.

practices.name: Seven quantitative message types pick the chart
practices.source: Stephen Few, 'Eenie, Meenie, Minie, Moe: Selecting the Right Graph for Your Message', Perceptual Edge / Intelligent Enterprise
practices.what_is_shown: First name the relationship: nominal comparison, time series, ranking, part-to-whole, deviation, frequency distribution or correlation. Then encode it with position or length (points, lines, bars). Use lines for patterns over time, bars for individual values, and a reference line for deviation. Avoid size and color as quantity encodings.
practices.form: Chart-selection rule plus encoding guidance
practices.decision_types: Any decision whose evidence is quantitative. Deviation from a target or plan is the most decision-relevant type.
practices.concrete_example: For 'Did the change make runs cheaper than budget?', use a deviation chart: bars for each week's difference from budget, with a zero reference line.
practices.fails_when: The message is not quantitative (architecture, process, trade-offs), or several relationships are crammed into one chart. Few also says size and color make 'a visual puzzle'.

practices.name: Small multiples answer 'compared to what?'
practices.source: Edward Tufte, Envisioning Information (1990), chapter 'Small Multiples'
practices.what_is_shown: The same small chart repeated across options, segments or time slices, with identical axes and scales, so the eye compares within one view. Tufte: 'At the heart of quantitative reasoning is a single question: Compared to what?'
practices.form: Grid of identical small charts
practices.decision_types: Choosing among options or spotting which segment differs. Works for medium stakes and reversible decisions where the decider must scan many cases.
practices.concrete_example: Three candidate deploy strategies, each shown as an identical mini line chart of error rate and latency over a 14-day trial, all on the same y-scale.
practices.fails_when: Scales differ between panels, there are too many panels to scan, or the decision needs one exact number rather than a pattern. The URL is Tufte's notebook, not the book itself; the quote comes from secondary summaries of the book.

practices.name: Sparklines and data inside sentences
practices.source: Edward Tufte, Beautiful Evidence (2006); 'Sparkline theory and practice' notebook
practices.what_is_shown: A word-sized trend line placed right next to the number or claim in the text or a table row. The reader sees the current value and its history together, which works against recency bias.
practices.form: Inline micro-chart in text or table
practices.decision_types: Monitoring and status decisions ('act or not') where history changes how a current number should be read
practices.concrete_example: 'Failed runs this week: 7 [sparkline of last 12 weeks]', so the reader sees at once whether 7 is a spike or normal. In the Iraq-slide critique Tufte proposed 14 sparklines to replace snapshot stoplights.
practices.fails_when: Exact values or scale are needed (sparklines have no axes), series need comparing on a common scale, or the rendering medium (chat, plain text) cannot draw them.

practices.name: Slopegraph for before/after
practices.source: Edward Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (1983) p.158; 'Slopegraphs for comparing gradients' notebook
practices.what_is_shown: Two columns, before and after. Each item is a labeled line joining its two values, so the slope shows the direction and size of change, and crossing lines show changes in rank.
practices.form: Table-graphic hybrid
practices.decision_types: Judging a change that already happened or is proposed (keep, roll back, extend). Fits reversible decisions with a few to about 20 items.
practices.concrete_example: Before and after a new review step: 6 metrics (time to merge, defects, cost per task, and so on) as labeled lines from 'old process' to 'new process'.
practices.fails_when: There are more than about 20 lines (spaghetti), the change has more than two time points, or the items sit on different units that cannot share one scale.

practices.name: Intense one-sheet summary matrix instead of slide decks
practices.source: Edward Tufte, 'PowerPoint Does Rocket Science--and Better Techniques for Technical Reports' (notebook, incl. NASA PRA review)
practices.what_is_shown: One dense summary early in the document: all risks ordered by size, each with its estimate and a comments column giving the background for that estimate, backed by more detailed arrays. Units and numbers are kept, not turned into adjectives. A detailed handout replaces bullet slides.
practices.form: Dense table / 11x17 technical report
practices.decision_types: High-stakes, hard-to-reverse engineering decisions (flight readiness, launch/no-launch)
practices.concrete_example: Tufte advised NASA's PRA group to replace 'chippy and twiddly' slides with a single ordered risk matrix plus a comments column. He also noted that the PRA missed on-ground analytic failures, which made up about 65% of observed shuttle risk.
practices.fails_when: Readers will not read dense material, or the matrix omits the risk category that actually matters, as the PRA did. A dense layout does not fix a wrong model.

practices.name: Outcome scatterplot for one causal question (Challenger case) and its counter-critique
practices.source: Edward Tufte, Visual Explanations (1997), chapter 'Visual and Statistical Thinking'; counter-analysis by Online Ethics Center (UVA)
practices.what_is_shown: Tufte's version: plot every past flight's damage against the causal variable (temperature) and mark where the planned launch sits on that axis, far outside past experience. The decision variable on one axis, all cases including those without damage, and the proposed action placed in context.
practices.form: Scatterplot of cases
practices.decision_types: Go/no-go decisions under time pressure where one causal variable dominates
practices.concrete_example: O-ring damage index against launch temperature for 24 flights, with the forecast 26-29F marked at the far left.
practices.fails_when: The chart uses data the decision-makers did not have. The UVA case argues Tufte's y-axis tracked the wrong effect and his x-axis used temperatures the engineers could not obtain. A clean chart built in hindsight can misattribute blame.

practices.name: Narrative memo read silently before discussion
practices.source: Jeff Bezos, 2017 Letter to Shareholders (Amazon)
practices.what_is_shown: A narratively structured memo of up to six pages with full sentences and the causal reasoning spelled out. Everyone reads it silently at the start of the meeting ('study hall'), then discussion follows. No slides.
practices.form: Long-form structured text
practices.decision_types: Big, consequential, hard-to-reverse strategy and product decisions where reasoning must be inspected
practices.concrete_example: A 6-page memo proposing a new service: customer problem, tenets, options, recommendation and risks. The meeting opens with 20 minutes of silent reading.
practices.fails_when: The decision is small or urgent (too costly to produce), or there is a quantitative pattern that prose hides. Tufte's own notebook entries, such as the Ballmer and Microsoft deck culture stories, show the same anti-slide stance.

practices.name: Big Idea and 3-minute story before any visual
practices.source: Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic, storytellingwithdata.com, 'what's the Big Idea?' and 'the 3-minute story' (after Nancy Duarte, Resonate)
practices.what_is_shown: One complete sentence that states the author's point of view, what is at stake, and the explicit ask, written before any chart. Each slide or section also carries its own big idea.
practices.form: Text structure (one sentence, then a 3-minute verbal story, then a storyboard)
practices.decision_types: Approval and resourcing decisions where the presenter has a recommendation
practices.concrete_example: Her example: 'The pilot summer learning program...was successful and...we recommend continuing...; please approve our budget for this program.'
practices.fails_when: The decision is genuinely open (exploratory, no recommendation yet), or the decider needs to weigh options neutrally. A one-sentence frame steers toward the author's preferred option.

practices.name: Declutter and focus: takeaway headline plus highlighted data plus annotation
practices.source: Ajani, Lee, Xiong, Nussbaumer Knaflic, Kemper, Franconeri, 'Declutter and Focus: Empirically Evaluating Design Guidelines for Effective Data Communication', IEEE TVCG
practices.what_is_shown: Strip non-critical gridlines, labels and color variety. Add a headline that states the pattern, color only the relevant subset, and attach a written annotation to it.
practices.form: Annotated chart
practices.decision_types: Explanatory communication of a known finding to a decider
practices.concrete_example: A line chart of weekly cost: all lines gray except the one repo that doubled, colored and labeled 'repo X doubled after switching models on Oct 3', with the headline 'One repo drives the cost rise'.
practices.fails_when: Results come from memory and recall tasks with undergraduates; the authors say they 'do not know whether these results would generalize' to other tasks. Focus also steers which pattern is remembered, which is bad when the highlighted pattern is the wrong one.

practices.name: Takeaway titles dominate what people remember (risk control)
practices.source: Kong, Liu, Karahalios, 'Trust and Recall of Information across Varying Degrees of Title-Visualization Misalignment', CHI 2019 (follow-up to 'Frames and Slants in Titles...', CHI 2018)
practices.what_is_shown: The finding: people's recall of a chart's message 'more frequently aligned with the titles than the visualization'. Most still judged the visualization impartial, even when the title contradicted it.
practices.form: Chart title (text) over a visualization
practices.decision_types: Any decision where an agent writes the headline over evidence it produced itself
practices.concrete_example: An agent titles a chart 'Migration reduced latency' while the chart shows a mixed result. The decider remembers 'reduced latency'.
practices.fails_when: This is a failure mode of practice 11, not a technique. Mitigate by having the title state the measured comparison neutrally and by showing the counter-evidence next to it.

practices.name: Dashboard means monitoring at a glance, not analysis
practices.source: Stephen Few, 'Dashboard Confusion Revisited', Perceptual Edge Visual Business Intelligence Newsletter
practices.what_is_shown: A dashboard is 'a visual display of the most important information needed to achieve one or more objectives; consolidated and arranged on a single screen so the information can be monitored at a glance'. Analysis needs a separate 'faceted analytical display' with global filters and brushing. Everything to be compared must sit within eye span, because short-term memory holds about four chunks.
practices.form: Single-screen dashboard vs interactive multi-view analysis
practices.decision_types: Operational, frequent, time-pressured decisions ('is anything off?'), as opposed to one-off investigative decisions
practices.concrete_example: An agent-pipeline status screen: one row per running task, with a bullet graph of elapsed time against budget and a red flag only when a threshold is crossed. Drilling down opens a separate analysis view.
practices.fails_when: Used for one-off strategic decisions, cluttered with gauges and decoration, or with charts that are not aligned in time so they cannot be compared.

practices.name: Bullet graph: actual vs target vs qualitative ranges
practices.source: Stephen Few, 'Bullet Graph Design Specification', Perceptual Edge
practices.what_is_shown: One linear bar for the actual value, a tick for the target, and shaded bands for poor, satisfactory and good, in a compact space. It replaces gauges and meters.
practices.form: Compact chart (dashboard element)
practices.decision_types: Monitoring decisions about whether a measure is on track against a target
practices.concrete_example: 'Task spend: $14 of $20 budget', with the band past $18 shaded as the danger zone.
practices.fails_when: There is no meaningful target or range. A bullet graph shows a single measure only, so comparing magnitudes across several of them misleads. Only the spec's search snippet was read, not the full spec, and the date is approximate.

practices.name: Weighted decision matrix / Pugh matrix
practices.source: ASQ, 'What is a Decision Matrix?' (adapted from The Quality Toolbox, 2nd ed.)
practices.what_is_shown: Options on one axis, weighted criteria on the other. Each option is rated, either on a consistent scale where high is always good or as -1/0/+1 against a baseline (Pugh). Ratings are multiplied by weights and summed. ASQ: the top score 'will not necessarily be the one to choose'; scores should prompt discussion and hybrid options.
practices.form: L-shaped table
practices.decision_types: Choosing one option from 3-7 by several criteria. Medium stakes, team decisions, after the list has been shortened.
practices.concrete_example: Choosing between GitHub Issues, Jira and a custom tracker. Criteria: owner effort (weight 5), agent API access (3), cost (2). Each option is rated against the current setup as the Pugh datum.
practices.fails_when: Ratings are opinions rather than collected data, criteria are worded inconsistently (cost where high is bad), raters' scores are averaged instead of discussed, or the ratings depend on guesses about the solution.

practices.name: Risk heatmap (likelihood x impact matrix), and why it misleads
practices.source: Louis Anthony Cox Jr., 'What's Wrong with Risk Matrices?', Risk Analysis 28(2):497-512
practices.what_is_shown: A colored grid of likelihood bands against impact bands with each risk placed in a cell. Cox's analysis shows the matrix can rank quantitatively different risks identically, and even reverse their order, because of coarse bins and subjective inputs.
practices.form: Heatmap grid
practices.decision_types: Prioritizing many risks quickly. It is a popular screening tool for low-precision triage.
practices.concrete_example: Risks of an auto-merge pipeline placed in a 5x5 grid. 'Silent data loss' (rare, catastrophic) and 'flaky test' (frequent, minor) land in the same orange cell.
practices.fails_when: It is used to allocate resources or rank risks of different kinds. Cox shows ratings 'do not necessarily support effective risk management'. Tufte makes a parallel critique of stoplight colors that 'dequantify data'. Better: show the numbers or ranges, then a separate judgment color. Only the abstract and metadata were reached, not the full text.

practices.name: Icon arrays / natural frequencies for probabilities
practices.source: Galesic, Garcia-Retamero, Gigerenzer, 'Using Icon Arrays to Communicate Medical Risks: Overcoming Low Numeracy', Health Psychology 28(2):210-216
practices.what_is_shown: A grid of 100 or 1,000 icons with affected cases colored, shown 'without action' and 'with action', alongside absolute (not relative) risk numbers. Both the numerator and the denominator are visible.
practices.form: Pictogram grid plus absolute numbers
practices.decision_types: Decisions under risk for non-specialists, such as whether to adopt a safeguard or accept a risk
practices.concrete_example: 'Without the review step, 8 of 100 merged tasks break main; with it, 3 of 100', drawn as two 10x10 grids.
practices.fails_when: The icon count shifts perception: risks looked less serious than in numbers, while 1,000 icons made the same risk and benefit look larger than 100 did. Choosing the denominator is therefore a framing choice. Absolute rather than relative framing alone gave a large effect (eta^2 .20 vs .06 for icons).

practices.name: Hypothetical outcome plots (animated draws) for uncertainty
practices.source: Hullman, Resnick, Adar, 'Hypothetical Outcome Plots Outperform Error Bars and Violin Plots for Inferences about Reliability of Variable Ordering', PLOS ONE 10(11)
practices.what_is_shown: Instead of error bars, the display animates individual plausible outcomes one frame at a time. Viewers count how often option A beats option B.
practices.form: Animated / interactive chart
practices.decision_types: Choosing between options whose outcomes are uncertain and overlapping (A vs B estimates, forecast-based plans)
practices.concrete_example: Two estimated completion times for options A and B, shown as 20 animated draws. The viewer sees that A finishes first in about 14 of 20.
practices.fails_when: The medium is static (chat, print), or the question is about a single quantity, where accuracy was similar for HOPs, error bars and violins. Evaluation in this field rarely measures decision quality.

practices.name: Zoomable architecture diagrams (C4) and a system-context diagram in the design doc
practices.source: Simon Brown, C4 model (c4model.com); Malte Ubl, 'Design Docs at Google' (industrialempathy.com)
practices.what_is_shown: Hierarchical diagrams at fixed zoom levels: system context (the system among the people and systems it touches), then containers, components and code. Google's design docs put a system-context diagram after 'Context and scope' and 'Goals and non-goals', so the reader places the new design in a landscape they already know. To show a change, the same view is drawn before and after, with added, removed and changed elements marked.
practices.form: Diagram (hierarchical, notation-independent)
practices.decision_types: Architecture changes reviewed by people of differing expertise. A non-specialist reads only the context level.
practices.concrete_example: System context, before: owner talks to one agent, which writes to the repo. After: owner talks to a router, which dispatches to 3 agents plus a reviewer before the repo. New boxes are outlined in a highlight color and the removed link is dashed.
practices.fails_when: Levels are mixed in one picture, there is no legend, or the delta is shown only as two separate pictures the reader must compare from memory. C4 itself defines no diff notation, so the before/after convention is local practice.

practices.name: Context, alternatives considered, consequences (design doc / ADR text structure)
practices.source: Michael Nygard, 'Documenting Architecture Decisions' (Cognitect); Google design-doc anatomy (industrialempathy.com)
practices.what_is_shown: Fixed order: Context (objective facts), Decision, Status, Consequences (the resulting context, good and bad). Google adds goals and non-goals and an 'Alternatives considered' section that shows the trade-offs of each rejected option. The doc's value lies in recording trade-offs, not in serving as an implementation manual.
practices.form: Structured text
practices.decision_types: Architecture and process decisions that must be recorded and revisited. Google says a doc is not worth writing when there were no trade-offs.
practices.concrete_example: An ADR titled 'Use GitHub Issues as tracker'. Context: two trackers in use. Decision. Consequences: Jira links break, and agents get native API access. Alternatives: Jira only, or Linear, each with its trade-off.
practices.fails_when: Used for small, obvious decisions (overhead), or when the alternatives are straw men. Google puts the useful length for big projects at 10-20 pages and suggests a 1-3 page mini doc for small ones.

practices.name: Now-Next-Later roadmap (timeline by confidence, not date)
practices.source: Janna Bastow, ProdPad, 'Why I Invented the Now-Next-Later Roadmap'
practices.what_is_shown: Three columns of initiatives (Now, Next, Later), ordered by certainty instead of fixed delivery dates and tied to outcomes. Detail decreases from left to right.
practices.form: Column timeline / board
practices.decision_types: Sequencing and prioritization decisions under uncertainty that will be revised later
practices.concrete_example: Now: tracker integration. Next: auto-merge for small tasks. Later: parallel agents across repos. Each card shows the outcome it targets.
practices.fails_when: Hard external deadlines or dependencies need real dates (a Gantt chart fits better). Without outcomes on the cards it turns into an undated wishlist. This is a vendor's own framing, so treat it as practice, not evidence.

practices.name: Start from the task abstraction: what, why, how (nested model)
practices.source: Tamara Munzner, Visualization Analysis and Design (2014); 'A Nested Model of Visualization Design and Validation' (IEEE TVCG 2009); UBC course slides
practices.what_is_shown: Design in four nested levels: the domain situation, then the data and task abstraction (what data, why the user looks: compare, locate, identify outliers, decide), then the visual encoding and interaction idiom, then the algorithm. Each level gets its own validation; an error at an upper level cannot be fixed below it.
practices.form: Design framework (meta-practice)
practices.decision_types: Designing a repeated decision display, such as the template for how a pipeline presents every decision
practices.concrete_example: Before designing a 'decision card', write down the task abstraction: 'owner must compare 2-3 options on cost, reversibility and risk, then choose'. Only then pick a matrix, a chart or text.
practices.fails_when: It is skipped. Teams jump to chart types (the 'how') without stating the 'why', and validate with satisfaction ratings instead of the decision outcome.

principles: Match the form to the task, not to the content type: graphs for patterns, trends and comparisons (spatial tasks), tables for exact lookups (symbolic tasks), prose for causal arguments and trade-offs (Vessey 1991; Speier 2006; Few 2004).

Every number needs a comparison next to it: the previous period, the target, the alternative, or the 'do nothing' baseline. Small multiples, sparklines, slopegraphs, bullet graphs and before/after icon arrays all do this (Tufte: 'Compared to what?').

Show the change, not two states: put before and after in one view (slopegraph, delta-highlighted diagram, Pugh matrix against a datum) rather than making the reader compare from memory. Short-term memory holds about 4 chunks (Few 2007).

Lead with the conclusion and the ask in one complete sentence, then give the evidence (Knaflic/Duarte Big Idea; Amazon memo). But a takeaway title overrides what the chart shows in memory (Kong 2019), so the title must be checked against the data.

Do not turn numbers into colors or adjectives: stoplights and risk heatmaps can rank risks wrongly (Cox 2008; Tufte on stoplights). Show the number or range, then give the judgment as a separate mark.

For probabilities, use absolute frequencies ('3 of 100') with a visible denominator. Pictograms help people with low numeracy, but the size of the denominator shifts perceived seriousness (Galesic 2009).
Uncertainty needs its own form: animated or enumerated outcomes beat error bars for 'which option is better' (Hullman 2015). Static medium: say 'A beats B in about 14 of 20 scenarios'.
Separate monitoring from analysis: a dashboard answers 'is anything off?' at a glance; investigation needs its own drill-down view (Few 2007).
Diagrams for system changes need fixed zoom levels and a legend. A non-specialist gets the system-context level plus a marked delta, and component detail sits behind a click (C4; Google design docs).

Show the alternatives and their trade-offs, not just the chosen path. 'Alternatives considered' and 'Consequences' are the parts of a decision record that readers keep using (Google design docs; Nygard ADR).
Dense, data-rich single views beat fragmented slides for high-stakes technical decisions (Tufte NASA PRA; Amazon six-pagers). But the density must cover the risk that actually matters.
Design starts from the task abstraction (what decision, what comparison) and is validated by decision quality, not by satisfaction (Munzner nested model; Hullman et al. survey).
Hindsight charts can mislead: a clean causal chart must use only the information available at decision time (UVA critique of Tufte's Challenger scatterplot).
numbers: Hullman et al. survey of 86 uncertainty-visualization studies: only 14 of 372 coded evaluation paths (3.8%) measured decision quality. Most measured accuracy or satisfaction.

Galesic et al. 2009: absolute vs relative risk format effect eta^2 = .20; adding icon arrays independently eta^2 = .06. Icon-array risks rated less serious than numeric ones (9.1 vs 10.3 on a 15-point scale). Screenings rated more helpful with 1,000 icons than with 100 (9.7 vs 8.9).
Speier 2006: graphs gave faster decisions on all task types except complex-symbolic, where graphs and tables were equal in time.
Few 2007: short-term memory holds about 4 chunks, so everything to be compared should sit within eye span.
Tufte on the shuttle PRA: on-ground analytic failures account for about 1.3 of 2.0 accidents in 113 flights, so about 65% of observed risk was not covered by the risk model.
Tufte on the ET-119 Flight Readiness Review: about 10 of 33 slides were content-free. He estimates the content could fit on 4 pages of 11x17 paper.
Amazon: memos up to 6 pages, read silently at the start of each meeting (Bezos 2017 letter).

Google design docs: 10-20 pages is the sweet spot for larger projects; 1-3 page mini design docs for incremental work. A design doc is probably worth it if 3 or more of 5 checklist questions are 'yes'.
Hullman 2015: with HOPs, judgments about two and three quantities were 'much more accurate' than with error bars and violin plots; single-quantity accuracy was similar.
Cox 2008 'What's wrong with risk matrices?' has about 1,668 citations (Google Scholar snippet); Vessey 1991 cognitive fit has about 2,000 citations.
not_found: No controlled study found that compares before/after architecture-delta diagrams with prose for non-specialist deciders. Searched 'architecture diagram before and after highlight changed components' via serper; results were tutorials and one INCOSE model-review paper (Cederbladh 2025), which was not read.
C4 (c4model.com home page) defines zoom levels but no diff/delta notation. The before/after-with-highlights convention is unstandardized practice.

Full texts not read because publishers' bot walls or cookie gates blocked them: Vessey 1991 (Wiley), Cox 2008 (PubMed/Wiley; only metadata on RePEc), Kong 2018 CHI (Semantic Scholar check). Claims for these rely on abstracts and search snippets. The Vessey-Galletta 1991 PDF was a scanned image with no text layer.
Stephen Few's 'Show Me the Numbers' table-vs-graph rules were seen only via third-party summaries, not the book; the 2004 Perceptual Edge article was used instead.
Bullet Graph Design Spec was not opened (search snippet only); the date is approximate.
Tufte's small-multiples quote comes from secondary summaries of Envisioning Information; the book itself was not read.
Munzner's book was not read; only the UBC course slides and summaries were found.
Not searched: flow/swimlane (as-is vs to-be) process diagrams with primary sources, video formats, and Klein's premortem as a visual.

practices.name: SBAR (Situation-Background-Assessment-Recommendation)
practices.source: Institute for Healthcare Improvement; developed by M. Leonard, D. Bonacum, S. Graham at Kaiser Permanente Colorado
practices.date: c. 2002-2003 (Kaiser introduction); IHI tool page undated
practices.what_is_shown: Fixed order: S = one-sentence statement of the problem; B = only the background relevant to that problem; A = the sender's own analysis and options ('what I think is going on'); R = the specific action requested ('what I want from you'). The sender must commit to an assessment and an ask; the receiver knows in advance where the ask will appear.
practices.form: Spoken or written script / worksheet with four labelled slots
practices.decision_types: Escalations to a senior who was not watching: urgent, moderately familiar, the decision is 'approve / come now / change course'. Fits when one sender owns the analysis and needs one action from one receiver.
practices.concrete_example: S: 'Bed 12's blood pressure dropped to 80/40 in the last hour.' B: 'Post-op day 1 after bowel resection, on morphine pump.' A: 'I think she may be bleeding.' R: 'I need you to see her in the next 15 minutes and want to send a CBC now.'
practices.fails_when: Situation needs several options compared (SBAR has one recommendation slot, no comparison); sender lacks the competence or confidence to assess, so A and R are left empty; used as a ritual form for routine updates, where the structure adds length without a decision.

practices.name: I-PASS handoff (illness severity first, receiver read-back)
practices.source: Starmer AJ et al., I-PASS Study Group, New England Journal of Medicine 371:1803-1812
practices.what_is_shown: I = Illness severity as a three-level label first (stable / 'watcher' / unstable); P = patient summary; A = action list with owners and timing; S = situation awareness and contingency plans written as if-then ('if X happens, do Y'); S = synthesis by receiver, who restates the essentials and asks questions. Paired with a written handoff document and training.
practices.form: Mnemonic-structured verbal handoff plus a printed/electronic written summary; closed-loop read-back
practices.decision_types: Transfer of responsibility between shifts; many items, varying urgency; the receiver must later act alone. Fits recurring, moderately time-pressured decisions where the next decider was not present.
practices.concrete_example: 'Watcher. 6-year-old with pneumonia on day 2 of antibiotics. To do: recheck oxygen at 2 a.m. If saturation drops below 90%, start high-flow and call the ICU fellow.' Receiver: 'So: watcher, oxygen check at 2, below 90 means high-flow and ICU call. Correct?'
practices.fails_when: Receiver synthesis is skipped (no check of understanding); contingencies are vague ('watch him'); the written document goes stale. Measured result across 9 hospitals: medical errors fell 23% (24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions) and preventable adverse events 30% (4.7 to 3.3), so effect depends on the whole bundle, not the mnemonic alone.

practices.name: Ten Commandments for clinical decision support (single screen, change direction rather than stop, defaults)
practices.source: Bates DW et al., Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association 10(6)
practices.what_is_shown: Support is shown at the moment of the action (inside the order screen), fits on one screen, offers a concrete alternative rather than only 'don't', pre-selects the recommended option as the default, asks for extra data only when indispensable, and is tracked by acceptance rate.
practices.form: In-workflow interactive prompt with a pre-filled default and an override path
practices.decision_types: High-frequency, routine, reversible choices made inside an existing workflow (dose, frequency, test choice), where the right answer is mostly known in advance.
practices.concrete_example: Changing the default ondansetron frequency on the order screen from four to three times daily moved four-times-daily orders from 89.7% to 13.7% within four weeks; suggestions to cancel an abdominal x-ray with no alternative were accepted only 5% of the time, while suggestions to change views were accepted almost half the time.
practices.fails_when: The guideline does not fit on one screen (users abandon it; effect becomes a mere barrier); the prompt says 'stop' with no alternative; too many low-value prompts train users to override (they target over ~60% acceptance for action-oriented prompts and prune the rest); support is bypassed by order paths that skip the screen.

practices.name: Tiering alerts by severity (only the top tier interrupts)
practices.source: Paterno MD et al., JAMIA 16(1):40-46
practices.what_is_shown: Drug-interaction alerts are sorted into tiers: the most severe tier is hard-stop/interruptive, the middle tier is interruptive but overridable, lower tiers are passive information. The decider sees severity encoded in how intrusive the alert is, not only in its text.
practices.form: Graded UI intrusiveness (modal hard stop vs. dismissible dialog vs. inline note)
practices.decision_types: High-volume streams of warnings where most items are low risk but a few are critical; reversible-to-irreversible mix.
practices.concrete_example: Two hospitals with the same alert knowledge base: compliance with interaction alerts was 29% at the site with tiered alerts versus 10% at the non-tiered site, where every alert looked equally important.
practices.fails_when: Tier assignment drifts upward ('everything is critical'), recreating the flat alert stream; low tiers are never reviewed, so a mis-tiered serious alert is never seen.

practices.name: Alarm budget and priority distribution (alarm fatigue control)
practices.source: The Joint Commission, Sentinel Event Alert 50; EEMUA 191 / ANSI/ISA-18.2 / IEC 62682 targets as summarized by an ISA-18.2 committee member (VanCamp, Chemical Engineering)
practices.what_is_shown: The operator sees only events that need a timely response. Informational messages, reminders and redundant consequential alarms are removed from the alarm channel. Priorities are rationed so that roughly 80% of annunciated alarms are low, 15% medium and 5% high, and priority is set by consequence of inaction combined with time available to act.
practices.form: Alarm list plus management KPIs (rate per 10 minutes, flood percentage, top-10 sources, stale alarms) reviewed as timeline and pie charts
practices.decision_types: Continuous monitoring by one operator over many signals; urgent, time-critical responses; any channel that pushes interruptions to a human.
practices.concrete_example: Targets: about 1-2 new alarms per 10 minutes per operator (action limit above 3); a 'flood' is more than 10 alarms in 10 minutes and should occur in under 1% of periods. Joint Commission: an estimated 85-99% of hospital alarm signals require no clinical intervention, which leads staff to silence or ignore alarms.
practices.fails_when: The alarm system is used for FYI messages or maintenance reminders; a single upset fires many redundant alarms (pump trip plus low flow plus low pressure); priorities are set by worst imaginable outcome, skewing toward 'critical'; suppression hides stale alarms without fixing the cause. Averages hide floods, so a monthly average can look acceptable while peak periods are unmanageable.

practices.name: Three-level flight-deck alerting hierarchy (warning / caution / advisory)
practices.source: 14 CFR 25.1322 Flightcrew alerting (FAA), with guidance in AC 25.1322-1
practices.what_is_shown: Each alert gives the information needed to identify the condition and determine the action. Level is defined by response timing: warning = immediate awareness and immediate response; caution = immediate awareness, subsequent response; advisory = awareness, maybe later response. Warnings and cautions use two senses (sound plus light), red and amber are reserved for alerting only, alerts disappear when the condition clears, and any suppression of an alert must itself be clearly announced.
practices.form: Color-coded text messages (EICAS) plus aural/tactile cues; regulated color convention
practices.decision_types: Time-critical, high-stakes operational decisions where several alerts may arrive at once and must be ranked instantly.
practices.concrete_example: A red 'CABIN ALTITUDE' warning with aural alert means act now (memory items); an amber 'PACK L' caution means run the checklist once the flight path is under control; a cyan/white advisory means note it for planning.
practices.fails_when: Two authorities give contradicting commands: at Überlingen (2002) the Tu-154 crew followed the controller's 'descend' instead of the TCAS resolution advisory 'climb', and collided (BFU report). Also fails when nuisance alerts are frequent, or the same urgency colors are reused for non-alert functions.

practices.name: Non-normal checklist anatomy (condition, objective, memory items, 'Confirm' on irreversible steps, deferred and optional information)
practices.source: Boeing 777 Flight Crew Operations Manual, Checklist Instructions - Non-Normal Checklists (NTSB docket DCA15FA185, Attachment 14)
practices.what_is_shown: In order: title matching the alert; a one-line condition statement (what happened); an objective statement (what doing this achieves); memory items above a dashed line (done before reading); reference items; decision points marked 'Choose one'; precautions before risky actions; an inoperative-items table with consequences for planning; deferred items moved to later phase checklists; 'additional information' at the end that 'does not need to be read'. Steps that are hard to undo (fuel control switch, fire switch, thrust lever) carry 'Confirm' and need verbal agreement of both pilots.
practices.form: Structured printed and electronic checklist; sensed items turn green automatically; branching with explicit choice symbol
practices.decision_types: Abnormal situations with a known procedure, moderate time pressure, a mix of reversible and irreversible actions, two-person crews.
practices.concrete_example: Engine fire: memory items done immediately; then the pilot monitoring reads the title and objective; before pulling the fire switch the checklist says 'Confirm', so both pilots verbally agree on which engine; 'Plan to land at the nearest suitable airport' appears as a planning item; optional background sits after the end.
practices.fails_when: The situation is not covered or several failures combine (the manual itself says the captain must then use judgment and that troubleshooting beyond the checklist can make things worse); the crew starts the checklist before the flight path is stable; confirm steps are rushed and the wrong engine is shut down.

practices.name: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (pause points, team check)
practices.source: Haynes AB et al., New England Journal of Medicine 360:491-499
practices.what_is_shown: Three short pause points (before anesthesia, before incision, before the patient leaves the room). At each, a named coordinator reads a short list aloud and team members confirm; the list includes team introductions and each member stating anticipated critical events. Mostly DO-CONFIRM: the team works from memory and the pause catches omissions.
practices.form: One-page checklist read aloud at fixed moments; verbal confirmation
practices.decision_types: Go / no-go gates before irreversible steps in routine high-stakes work by experts who know the content but skip items under pressure.
practices.concrete_example: Before incision: confirm patient, site, procedure; surgeon states critical steps and expected blood loss; anesthetist states patient-specific concerns; nurse confirms sterility; antibiotic given in the last 60 minutes? In 8 hospitals, deaths fell from 1.5% to 0.8% and inpatient complications from 11.0% to 7.0%.
practices.fails_when: It is ticked without being read aloud or without the team pausing (box-checking); it grows long; the hierarchy discourages juniors from speaking; it is imposed without local adaptation.

practices.name: CRM captain's briefing (threats, plan, division of work, invitation to object)
practices.source: FAA Advisory Circular 120-51E, Crew Resource Management Training (Appendix 1 behavioral markers)
practices.what_is_shown: Before a phase of work: the most threatening safety situations, expected problems (weather, delays, inoperative systems), the plan tied to standard procedures, who does what (division of labor and workload), and an explicit invitation for questions and critique so that others will speak up later.
practices.form: Spoken, interactive pre-task briefing; assessed with behavioral markers
practices.decision_types: Decisions made in advance of a time-critical phase; team decisions where the person who notices a problem may not be the person who decides.
practices.concrete_example: 'Today's threats: gusty crosswind and a short runway. If we're not stable by 1,000 feet, we go around, no discussion. You're monitoring; call out any deviation. Questions or concerns?'
practices.fails_when: It becomes a monologue read by rote; it lists generic threats instead of today's; the authority gradient remains so steep that the invitation to object is not believed.

practices.name: Incident roles plus live incident state document (most important information at the top)
practices.source: Google, Site Reliability Engineering book, ch. 14 'Managing Incidents' and Appendix C 'Example Incident State Document'
practices.what_is_shown: One living document, top to bottom: one-line summary; status; where the command post is; who holds which role (incident commander, ops, planning, comms) and who is next; detailed status with exit criteria (what 'done' means, as measurable conditions); TODO list with DONE/TODO; timeline with most recent first. Stakeholders get periodic summaries from the comms lead instead of joining the debugging.
practices.form: Templated shared document plus role separation; email/IRC updates
practices.decision_types: Long-running, multi-person, high-pressure incidents where the decider changes over time (handoffs) and many people need status without interrupting the people fixing it.
practices.concrete_example: 'Summary: search service in cascading failure due to new item missing from the index. Status: active. IC: jennifer. Exit criteria: item indexed (TODO); within 99.99% availability and p99 < 100 ms for 30+ minutes (TODO).' Timeline below, newest first.
practices.fails_when: Nobody owns keeping it current (it decays into a chat log); roles are not separated, so the person fixing the system is also answering executives (the book's 'unmanaged incident'); handoff is implicit rather than an explicit 'you are now incident commander, okay?' with acknowledgement.

practices.name: Incident commander decision protocol (size-up, proposal plus 'any strong objections?', time-boxed assignment)
practices.source: PagerDuty Incident Response documentation, 'Incident Commander'
practices.what_is_shown: Size-up: 'What's wrong?' and 'How big is it, is it escalating?'. Stabilize: 'What actions can we take? How risky are they?', then a decision stated as 'The proposal is X. Are there any strong objections?' (pause) 'Hearing none, we proceed.' Tasks go to a named person with a time box and acknowledgement. Periodic status: severity, believed cause, open questions and when answers are due, next public update time. Yes/no questions demand yes/no answers.
practices.form: Spoken protocol with scripted phrases; Slack channel plus call
practices.decision_types: Urgent, uncertain, reversible-enough operational choices where waiting is worse than a wrong choice ('Making the wrong decision is better than making no decision').
practices.concrete_example: 'The proposal is to roll back the 14:02 deploy. Strong objections?' ... 'Bob, roll back web tier; I'll check back in 3 minutes. Understood?' Executive asks for a customer spreadsheet: 'We can either get you that list or fix the incident. Not both.'
practices.fails_when: Senior people override without taking command ('executive swoop'); the call debates severity mid-incident; tasks are thrown out as 'can someone...' (bystander effect); concise jargon replaces clear statements ('clear is better than concise').

practices.name: Symptom-first pages with cause summary, sub-critical issues routed away from the pager
practices.source: Rob Ewaschuk, 'My Philosophy on Alerting' (Google SRE), basis for SRE book ch. 6
practices.what_is_shown: A page interrupts only for something urgent, important, actionable and real, phrased as the user-visible symptom with magnitude and window; underneath, a terse 'also firing' list of cause-level signals so the reader can match symptom to likely cause in a glance; a short playbook note. Things that need attention soon but not now go to tickets or a daily report with a named owner.
practices.form: Short structured alert text plus dashboard and playbook link; separate ticket/report channel
practices.decision_types: Interrupt decisions: is this worth waking someone up? Separates 'act now' from 'act this week'.
practices.concrete_example: 'TooMany500StatusCodes: served 10.7% 5xx in the last 3 minutes. Also firing: JanitorProcessNotKeepingUp, UserDatabaseShardDown, FreshnessIndexBehind' (makes the database the obvious suspect).
practices.fails_when: Alerts are less than 50% accurate (the author calls them broken); the sub-critical channel has no owner and becomes an ignored mailing list; symptoms appear too late (quota exhaustion), so a predictive cause alert is needed.

practices.name: Pre-built decision trees for recurring incident decisions
practices.source: incident.io blog, '7 ways teams are using incident.io's Decision Flows' (A. Debenham)
practices.what_is_shown: During an incident, the responder invokes a guided question sequence for a known recurring decision (what severity is this, is it us or the vendor, update the status page or not, escalate to legal/security or not, can we close). Each answer leads to the next question and finally to a decision, sometimes with pre-approved wording to paste.
practices.form: Interactive question-by-question flow in Slack
practices.decision_types: Recurring, rule-based decisions that are argued about in the moment but could be agreed in calm conditions; medium stakes.
practices.concrete_example: '/incident decision' -> 'Is customer data exposed?' yes -> 'Is it more than one customer?' yes -> 'Page the privacy lead and use status page template B.'
practices.fails_when: The situation does not fit the tree; trees are long flowcharts for rare cases (Ewaschuk warns detailed flowcharts mean time spent documenting instead of fixing); trees are not maintained as rules change.

practices.name: Flight rules: decisions made in advance
practices.source: IAEA / UN COPUOS, Safety Framework for Nuclear Power Source Applications in Outer Space (definition used by NASA)
practices.what_is_shown: A collection of pre-planned decisions for nominal and off-nominal situations, written and agreed before the mission, to minimize real-time decision making. In the moment, the decider sees which rule's conditions are met and the pre-agreed action; debate happened earlier, with full rationale recorded in the rule.
practices.form: Text rulebook with condition-action rules and rationale; referenced during operations
practices.decision_types: Foreseeable high-stakes, time-critical decisions; especially irreversible ones where calm deliberation in advance beats improvisation.
practices.concrete_example: 'If a second fuel cell fails, abort the mission and land at the next opportunity' (illustrative of the condition-action form); the console shows the condition, the controller cites the rule, the flight director confirms.
practices.fails_when: The situation was not foreseen (Apollo 13-type novel failures) or several rules conflict; rules are applied mechanically when their assumptions do not hold.

practices.name: Army decision briefing (problem and recommendation first, format scaled to decider familiarity)
practices.source: US Army FM 6-0, Commander and Staff Organization and Operations, Appendix B (Figure B-2)
practices.what_is_shown: Introduction: 'This is a decision briefing', problem statement, recommendation ('Of three courses of action we recommend COA 1'). Main body: facts (positive and negative), assumptions (to be validated later), options, evaluation criteria, comparison of options against criteria, why the recommendation wins. Closing: restate recommendation, request the decision explicitly, confirm everyone understands it; bring the implementation document to sign. If the decider is unfamiliar with the problem, the full format is used; if familiar, a short decision-paper form (problem, essential background, impacts, recommendation).
practices.form: Oral briefing with slides, or written decision paper; comparison matrix of options vs criteria
practices.decision_types: Deliberate but time-bounded decisions with several options and trade-offs; fits both familiar and unfamiliar deciders by scaling depth.
practices.concrete_example: 'Sir, this is a decision briefing. Problem: select a brigade for the tasking. Recommendation: COA 1.' Then a criteria-by-COA comparison table, then 'Request your decision on COA 1.'
practices.fails_when: The recommendation is buried at the end; assumptions are presented as facts; the comparison criteria are chosen to favor the preferred option; the briefing ends without an explicit decision.

practices.name: Commander's critical information requirements (CCIR) and commander's intent
practices.source: US Army FM 6-0 (CCIR, para 5-40 to 5-44); ADP 6-0 Mission Command (intent: purpose, key tasks, end state)
practices.what_is_shown: The decider states in advance which specific pieces of information they need, each tied to a specific decision they expect to make; staff deliver those immediately and filter everything else. In the other direction, the decider gives subordinates the purpose, key tasks and desired end state so they can decide locally without asking.
practices.form: Short written list of information requirements and a short intent statement in the order
practices.decision_types: Operations where many people collect information and few decide; fits delegation: what must come up versus what can be decided below.
practices.concrete_example: CCIR: 'Notify me immediately if the bridge at X is destroyed' (that triggers the decision to switch to the alternate route). Intent: 'Purpose: keep the supply route open. End state: convoy through by 0600.'
practices.fails_when: CCIRs are generic or never updated (FM 6-0 says they must change with the situation); the list is long, so everything becomes 'critical'; intent is vague, so subordinates escalate everything.

practices.name: Show the value against its limit and stop automatically (trading desk risk monitoring)
practices.source: US SEC, Order Instituting Proceedings, In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC, Release No. 70694
practices.what_is_shown: What failed: the position monitor (PMON) showed positions but not the limits, so 'the person viewing PMON had to know the applicable limits'; it had no automated alerts and was not linked to order entry. 97 automated emails flagging the faulty deployment ('Power Peg disabled') arrived before market open, but they were not designed as alerts and were not reviewed. The lesson: display exposure next to its limit, alert on breach, and block automatically at hard limits.
practices.form: Dashboard (position vs limit), alert channel, automated hard stop
practices.decision_types: Machine-speed risk where human reaction is too slow; financial exposure decisions; kill-switch decisions.
practices.concrete_example: In 45 minutes Knight accumulated about $3.5 billion long and $3.15 billion short and lost over $460 million; a display reading 'gross position 3.5B / limit X (breached)' with an automatic stop would have made the decision obvious.
practices.fails_when: (This entry is itself the failure case.) Warning signals go to an unmonitored mailbox; the display shows raw numbers without the threshold; humans are the only control in a system that moves faster than they can read.

practices.name: Headline states the finding; key number first (Columbia slide lesson)
practices.source: Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Vol. I, pp. 190-191, 'Engineering by Viewgraphs' (with E. Tufte's analysis)
practices.what_is_shown: Failure case. The Boeing slide's headline 'Review of Test Data Indicates Conservatism for Tile Penetration' referred to the model choice, not to predicted damage; the decisive fact (the debris was about 640 times larger than the test data used to calibrate the model) sat at the bottom; 11 sentences were split across six bullet levels; 'significant' was used 5 times with different meanings. Managers concluded there was no danger.
practices.form: Bulleted slide (the failure); the Board preferred technical papers to slides
practices.decision_types: Escalation of technical risk up a hierarchy to non-specialist deciders under schedule pressure.
practices.concrete_example: Tufte's suggested honest headline: 'Review of Test Data Indicates Irrelevance of Two Models'; the 640x out-of-range fact should lead.
practices.fails_when: (Failure case.) Compression into bullets drops caveats; vague quantifiers replace numbers; the headline says the comfortable thing; the decisive fact is placed last.

practices.name: National Early Warning Score (aggregate score mapped to response tiers)
practices.source: Royal College of Physicians, National Early Warning Score (NEWS) 2 report
practices.what_is_shown: Six routine vital signs are each scored 0-3 on a color-banded observation chart; the total maps directly to a response: low (0-4) ward-based response; medium (5-6) urgent review; high (7+) emergency response. A single parameter scoring 3 ('red score') triggers urgent review even if the total is low. The decider sees one number and the action attached to it, not raw vitals.
practices.form: Color-banded paper or electronic chart plus a score-to-action table
practices.decision_types: Escalation decisions made repeatedly by many staff of varying experience; detecting slow deterioration where trends matter more than single readings.
practices.concrete_example: Respiratory rate 24 (2), SpO2 93% (2), heart rate 112 (2): total 6, medium, so call a clinician for urgent review within the defined time.
practices.fails_when: Score replaces judgment (patients 'look wrong' but score low, or chronic conditions score high constantly); trigger thresholds are ignored because escalation capacity is lacking; observations are not repeated, so trends are missed.

practices.name: Recognition-primed decisions: experts decide by matching cases and mentally simulating one option
practices.source: Klein G., Calderwood R., Clinton-Cirocco A., 'Rapid Decision Making on the Fire Ground: The Original Study Plus a Postscript', Journal of Cognitive Engineering and Decision Making (original 1985 US Army Research Institute study)
practices.what_is_shown: Field interviews with fireground commanders found they rarely compared options side by side; they recognized the situation as typical of a known pattern (expected cues, plausible goals, typical action) and mentally simulated a single course of action, changing it only if the simulation showed a problem. Implication for presentation: show the analogous past case and how the proposed action is expected to unfold, plus the cues that would show it is going wrong.
practices.form: Case/analogue and narrative of the expected course ('this looks like X; we do Y; watch for Z')
practices.decision_types: Time-pressured decisions by experienced deciders in familiar domains; less suited to novel problems or novices, who need explicit comparison.
practices.concrete_example: 'This is like the March outage: same error pattern after a config push. Then a rollback fixed it in 6 minutes. If errors don't drop within 5 minutes of rollback, it's something else.'
practices.fails_when: The situation only looks familiar (false analogy); the decider lacks experience to recognize patterns; anomalous cues are explained away to fit the pattern.

principles: Lead with the urgency level and the ask, not the narrative: SBAR's S and R, I-PASS's illness severity, FM 6-0's problem and recommendation in the introduction, the SRE state document's summary and status at the top.

Encode urgency in the channel and form, not just in words: three regulated alert levels defined by response timing (immediate / subsequent / awareness), reserved colors, two senses for urgent items, and interruptive versus passive tiers. Tiering measurably raised alert compliance (29% vs 10%).

Ration interruptions with a budget: page only for what is urgent, actionable and real; route 'soon but not now' to tickets or reports with an owner; prune anything that is usually ignored. Alarm floods and 85-99% non-actionable alarms produce fatigue and missed critical signals.

Offer an alternative and pre-fill the recommended option; changing direction is accepted far more than stopping (ondansetron default change: 89.7% to 13.7% for the old regimen; 'don't order' accepted 5%).

Fit the decision support on one screen, but keep depth one step away: Boeing puts optional 'additional information' after the end of the checklist ('does not need to be read'); the Army scales briefing depth to how familiar the decider already is with the problem.

Mark irreversible steps differently: Boeing's 'Confirm' (two-person verbal agreement) on fuel cutoff and fire switches; WHO pause points before incision; Bezos's one-way versus two-way doors (Amazon 2015 shareholder letter) as a routing rule for how much deliberation a decision gets.
Decide recurring and foreseeable decisions in advance (flight rules, decision flows, if-then contingencies in I-PASS); at the moment of decision, show which pre-agreed condition is met.
Show the value against its threshold and the trend; a number without its limit forces the decider to remember the limit (Knight Capital PMON).
Headline must state the finding honestly and the decisive number must come first; bullets and vague quantifiers hide risk (Columbia slide).
Close the loop: receiver read-back (I-PASS synthesis), 'any strong objections?' polling, an explicit request for a decision at the end of a briefing, explicit handoff of command with acknowledgement.
Prefer clear over concise when brevity creates ambiguity (PagerDuty); one-line summaries work as the top layer, not as the whole message.

For experienced deciders under time pressure, a worked analogous case plus the expected course of action and the abort cues fits how they actually decide (recognition-primed decision); for novices or novel problems, show an explicit options-vs-criteria comparison (FM 6-0).
numbers: I-PASS (NEJM 2014, 9 hospitals): medical errors -23% (24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions); preventable adverse events -30% (4.7 to 3.3 per 100 admissions).
WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (NEJM 2009, 8 hospitals): death 1.5% to 0.8%; inpatient complications 11.0% to 7.0%.
Tiered drug-interaction alerts (JAMIA 2009): compliance 29% at the tiered site vs 10% at the non-tiered site.

Bates 2003: default change moved ondansetron four-times-daily orders from 89.7% to 13.7% in four weeks (about $250,000 saved in year one); 'no x-ray' suggestion accepted 5%; changing views suggestion accepted almost 50%; target acceptance above about 60% for action-oriented prompts; pharmacists overrode a third of life-threatening interaction alerts in a cited study.
Joint Commission Sentinel Event Alert 50 (2013): an estimated 85-99% of hospital alarm signals do not require clinical intervention.

EEMUA 191 / ISA-18.2 targets: about 1-2 alarms per 10 minutes per operator (at most 12 per hour; action limit above 18 per hour); flood = more than 10 alarms in 10 minutes, under 1% of periods; priority mix about 80% low / 15% medium / 5% high; top-10 sources under about 5% of alarms (action limit 20%).
Ewaschuk (Google SRE): alerts less than 50% accurate are broken; 10% false positives already merit review.
Knight Capital (SEC 2013): 97 unread error emails before the open; 45 minutes of runaway orders; about $3.5B long and $3.15B short; over $460M loss.
Columbia slide (CAIB 2003): debris about 640 times larger than the calibration test data (later analysis: about 400 times); 'significant' used 5 times; 11 sentences across 6 bullet levels.
NEWS2 (RCP 2017): total 5-6 = urgent review, 7 or more = emergency response; any single parameter scoring 3 = urgent review.
Bezos 2016 letter: most decisions should be made with about 70% of the information you wish you had.
not_found: No primary source found on how trading-desk screens are laid out for traders' decisions (limit utilization displays, P&L heat maps); the only trading-floor practice covered is the Knight Capital SEC failure finding. Searched serper; did not check FIA or exchange vendor documentation.

NEJM and PubMed pages were blocked (bot check / cookies), so the I-PASS and WHO checklist figures come from NEJM abstract snippets and press summaries of the same papers, not the full text read directly.
Did not read the full Joint Commission Sentinel Event Alert 50 or the original EEMUA 191 / ISA-18.2 standards (paywalled); alarm targets come from an ISA-18.2 committee member's article.
Did not read ADP 6-0 directly; commander's-intent wording (purpose, key tasks, end state) is from search snippets of ADP 6-0. Did not read AR 25-50 (BLUF) directly.
Did not read the full NEWS2 report; thresholds are from search snippets of the RCP report and a PMC review.

No primary-source controlled study found that compares presentation forms (chart vs text vs case example) for one-off strategic decisions under time pressure; the measured evidence is all about alerts, handoffs and checklists for recurring decisions.
The Columbia CAIB pages were read from a hosted copy of the report pages, not from NASA's site.
The NASA flight rules example in the practice entry is illustrative of the form, not quoted from an actual flight rule; the definition is from the IAEA/UN safety framework.
Did not cover video or interactive simulation formats for decision support; no primary source on them turned up in these fields.
fetchira worked throughout via serper; firecrawl was rate-limited once (Paterno full text not read; figure from the abstract snippet).

practices.name: Worked example before abstract rule (worked-example effect)
practices.source: Sweller & Cooper 1985 (Cognition and Instruction); boundary: Kalyuga, Chandler, Tuovinen & Sweller 2001 and Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller 2003 (expertise reversal effect); summarized by MIT Teaching + Learning Lab
practices.what_is_shown: Problem statement, then each solution step in full, then the result. The reader studies a finished case before facing a new problem of the same kind. Novices get the full worked example; experts get the bare problem.
practices.form: Example/case: a step-by-step worked solution as structured text
practices.decision_types: Unfamiliar decision types where the decider does not yet know the pattern (first time choosing a merge strategy, first deploy policy). Low-to-medium stakes, recurring decisions where the decider must later decide alone.
practices.concrete_example: Instead of 'Recommend squash-merge for small PRs', show one real PR: 14 commits -> squash -> single commit on main -> how revert looked afterwards. Then ask about the new PR.
practices.fails_when: The decider is already expert in this type of decision. Then the worked example is redundant, adds load, and solving or deciding directly works better (expertise reversal effect, Kalyuga et al. 2003, psycnet record 2003-04803-004). It also fails when the example is surface-similar but structurally different from the current case.

practices.name: Two contrasting cases side by side, with an explicit 'what is common' prompt (analogical encoding)
practices.source: Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner, 'Analogical Learning in Negotiation Teams: Comparing Cases Promotes Learning and Transfer', Academy of Management Learning & Education 2(2):119-127
practices.what_is_shown: Two short (~225-word) concrete cases from different surface contexts that share one deep principle. The decider is asked 'what are the key parallels', not 'analyze each'. After that comes the principle (the 'moral of the story') and then the new situation.
practices.form: Example/case pair, comparison prompt, then principle
practices.decision_types: Recurring judgment calls where the decider must recognize the pattern later without help, for example 'this is another case of an irreversible migration'. Medium stakes, unfamiliar principle.
practices.concrete_example: Show case A: a DB migration rolled out behind a flag. Show case B: a pricing change rolled out to 5% of users. Ask what both have in common: reversibility bought by a staged rollout. Then present the current decision.
practices.fails_when: The cases are given one at a time or analyzed separately. In that arm, separate-case teams formed the value-creating contract in 22% of negotiations, no better than no training (23%), while comparison teams reached 40%. In earlier individual studies the rates were 24% vs 58%. It also fails when the two cases share misleading surface commonalities or play different roles. People do not compare spontaneously; the prompt to compare is the active ingredient.

practices.name: Simulated experience instead of a described statistic
practices.source: Hogarth & Soyer, 'Using Simulated Experience to Make Sense of Big Data', MIT Sloan Management Review; 'Sequentially simulated outcomes', J. Exp. Psych: General 140(3) 2011; 'Providing information for decision making: Contrasting description and simulation', JARMAC 4(3) 2015
practices.what_is_shown: The decider sets the inputs of an option (for example X1, X2, X3), presses 'simulate', and sees one sampled outcome. They repeat as often as they like and can then average or histogram the draws. They meet the outcomes one at a time before seeing any summary number.
practices.form: Interactive simulation (sampled outcomes, optional histogram)
practices.decision_types: Decisions under uncertainty with skewed or noisy outcomes: forecasts, investments, rollout risk, market entry. Moderate to high stakes, statistically non-intuitive. Not needed for simple probabilistic situations.
practices.concrete_example: For 'auto-merge PRs when CI is green': a button that replays 100 simulated weeks from past data. Each run shows how many bad merges slipped through that week (0, 0, 3, 0, 1...), not just 'expected 0.4/week'.
practices.fails_when: Few draws are sampled, so intuitions follow sampling noise; the authors' remedy is many observations per input. Also when the underlying model is biased, because the simulation inherits its blind spots. It is costly to build, and it frustrates deciders who want one precise answer.

practices.name: Show the cloud, not just the fitted line (illustration over description)
practices.source: Soyer & Hogarth, 'The Illusion of Predictability: How Regression Statistics Mislead Experts', International Journal of Forecasting 28(3) 2012; recapped in MIT SMR
practices.what_is_shown: The raw individual outcomes (for example 250 data points) plotted with the average effect line, so the spread is visible next to the average. A table of coefficients alone hides the spread.
practices.form: Chart (scatter plot of individual outcomes)
practices.decision_types: Any decision based on an average effect where individual outcomes vary: 'this change improves latency on average', 'agents finish tasks 30% faster'.
practices.concrete_example: Instead of 'agent PRs need 1.2 review rounds on average', plot every PR's review rounds as dots. The decider sees that some needed 6.
practices.fails_when: There are many interacting variables, so one static chart cannot hold them; the authors move to simulation there. Static charts also cannot show change over time without animation (they cite Rosling-style dynamic charts as a workaround). In the study, 257 economics scholars misjudged predictability from the standard regression description; the illustration corrected it.

practices.name: Personal stories / case narratives inside decision aids (patient decision aids)
practices.source: Shaffer et al., 'Do Personal Stories Make Patient Decision Aids More Effective? An Update from the International Patient Decision Aids Standards', Medical Decision Making 2021; earlier Bekker et al. 2013 (BMC Med Inform Decis Mak)
practices.what_is_shown: Balanced factual description of every option and its consequences, plus optional stories of people who chose each option. The IPDAS taxonomy separates narrative purpose (inform, engage, model behavior, persuade, comfort), content (process, experience, outcome) and valence.
practices.form: Example/case: testimonial or narrative text or video embedded in a structured decision aid
practices.decision_types: Preference-sensitive decisions with no single right answer, where the decider must imagine living with the consequences. High stakes, irreversible, unfamiliar.
practices.concrete_example: For a choice between two treatments: probabilities in an icon array, followed by one 'process' story per option (what the week after the procedure was like), with matched tone across options.
practices.fails_when: The story is an outcome narrative that is unrepresentative or unbalanced: narratives shift choices regardless of statistics, and people do not discount them for low source credibility. Bottom line of both reviews: evidence does not support making narratives a required component; they can harm informed choice.

practices.name: Identifiable single case vs statistics: the vivid-case distortion
practices.source: Small, Loewenstein & Slovic, 'Sympathy and callousness', Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 102 (2007)
practices.what_is_shown: Condition A: one named person (Rokia, 7) with photo. Condition B: aggregate statistics (millions in need). Condition C: the named person plus the statistics.
practices.form: Example/case vs numbers vs both
practices.decision_types: Warning for any decision where one vivid incident is shown next to base rates: incident-driven policy changes, 'one agent PR broke prod, so ban agent PRs'.
practices.concrete_example: Mean donations: identifiable victim $2.38, statistical victims $1.14, identifiable plus statistics $1.43. Adding the numbers to the case cut the case's pull rather than adding the statistics' weight.
practices.fails_when: A single case is used to carry a decision that should rest on frequency. Teaching people about the bias made them give less to the identifiable victim without giving more to the statistical one. A vivid case moves the decision; whether the move is right depends on whether the case is representative, so the case must come with its base rate.

practices.name: Premortem (prospective hindsight on a plan already presented)
practices.source: Klein, 'Performing a Project Premortem', HBR Sept 2007; tested in Veinott, Klein & Wiggins, ISCRAM 2010; mechanism from Mitchell, Russo & Pennington 1989
practices.what_is_shown: 1) The plan. 2) The statement 'it is six months later and this plan failed completely'. 3) Two minutes for everyone to write reasons alone. 4) Reasons collected round-robin. 5) One mitigating action per person. 6) The plan is revised and the list revisited during execution.
practices.form: Text structure / facilitated exercise (failure story written in the past tense)
practices.decision_types: Go/no-go on a plan or project with high stakes and overconfidence risk, before commitment. Works under time pressure (about 10 minutes).
practices.concrete_example: Before approving 'agents push straight to main for small tasks': 'It is March; this was rolled back after an incident. Write why.' Answers such as 'flaky test passed', 'two agents edited the same file', 'no one read the diff' become guardrails.
practices.fails_when: The output is reduced confidence, not proven better plan quality. Veinott measured confidence (premortem -25 points vs -14 pro/con, -12 cons-only, about 0 for critique) and only weakly measured understanding, with students and a ready-made plan. The often-quoted '30% better at identifying reasons' overstates Mitchell 1989: the abstract reports effects of outcome certainty on explanation type, and Veinott describes the figure as about 30% more reasons, not more correct ones.

practices.name: Reference class forecasting / outside view (show the distribution of similar past cases first)
practices.source: Flyvbjerg, 'From Nobel Prize to Project Management: Getting Risks Right', Project Management Journal 37(3) 2006; Lovallo & Kahneman, 'Delusions of Success', HBR July 2003
practices.what_is_shown: 1) The reference class of past, similar projects. 2) The probability distribution of their outcomes (for example 40% of road projects overran by at most 10%, 80% by at most 32%). 3) Only then, where the current case sits against that distribution, and the required uplift for an acceptable risk level.
practices.form: Chart (cumulative distribution of past outcomes) plus the case's position on it
practices.decision_types: Estimates and commitments: cost, time, success probability. Recurring project types with available history; high stakes; prone to optimism and strategic misrepresentation.
practices.concrete_example: Before 'this refactor takes 2 days': show the last 20 refactors' estimate/actual ratios as a distribution (median 1.8x, 80th percentile 3x), then the estimate with an uplift.
practices.fails_when: No credible reference class exists (truly novel work), the class is too broad to compare or too narrow to be statistically meaningful, or data on past outcomes is missing. It is resisted by promoters who prefer the inside view. First practical use: the Edinburgh Tram, 2004, UK DfT uplifts.

practices.name: Amazon Working Backwards PR/FAQ
practices.source: Bryar & Carr (ex-Amazon), Working Backwards PR/FAQ instructions
practices.what_is_shown: Order: headline; subheading (exactly who the customer is and the benefit); summary with launch date; problem paragraph from the customer's view; solution, including 'today customers use x, y, z, which fall short because...'; spokesperson and hypothetical customer quote; external FAQ; internal FAQ (TAM, unit economics, risks, 'top three reasons this will not succeed', 'what must be true'). Read silently for 15-20 minutes, then discussed.
practices.form: Text structure: a narrative from the future (as-if-launched press release) plus Q&A
practices.decision_types: New product or initiative go/no-go; high stakes, partly irreversible investment, unfamiliar territory. Not for small reversible changes.
practices.concrete_example: Their car example: the 'Phoenix 400' release (no better than rivals) is discarded before the FAQ. The 'Excel 850' (850-mile range, $19,000) is a compelling destination, and its FAQ lists the unsolved engineering problems.
practices.fails_when: It is used to sell rather than seek the truth, or the competition and current solutions are discounted. Teams skip iterations: good PR/FAQs took months and many drafts for AWS. It fits poorly when the decision is about internal mechanics without a customer-facing outcome.

practices.name: Basecamp Shape Up pitch: one specific 'status quo' story plus appetite plus fat-marker sketch
practices.source: Ryan Singer, Shape Up (Basecamp), chapter 'Write the Pitch'
practices.what_is_shown: 1) Problem: ideally 'a single specific story that shows why the status quo doesn't work', which becomes the baseline to test fitness against. 2) Appetite (2 or 6 weeks). 3) Solution as breadboards, embedded or annotated fat-marker sketches, adding visual detail only for the 'linchpin' part. 4) Rabbit holes. 5) No-gos. Posted asynchronously; comments poke holes; the decision happens at the betting table.
practices.form: Text structure plus rough sketches; sometimes videos of the problem and a data visualization
practices.decision_types: Prioritizing what to build next (betting); medium stakes, time-boxed, reversible by cycle. Good for the 'how it was / how it will be' contrast.
practices.concrete_example: Their to-do grouping pitch opens with a screenshot of the workaround users built in the current design, then sketches the grouping. The notifications pitch opens with two videos demonstrating the problem.
practices.fails_when: The solution is over-specified with wireframes (it boxes in designers and drifts into color and layout debates), or the pitch has a solution with no problem or a problem with no solution. Hand-drawn breadboards look like 'a soup of words and arrows' to people who were not there, so they must be redrawn and labeled.

practices.name: GV Design Sprint: storyboard, then a realistic prototype tested with five customers
practices.source: GV (Knapp, Zeratsky, Kowitz), The Design Sprint
