practices.what_is_shown: Monday: long-term goal and map. Tuesday: competing sketches. Wednesday: decision, then a step-by-step storyboard of the customer's path. Thursday: a realistic facade prototype. Friday: watch five target customers use it. The decision-maker sees real reactions to a concrete future product, not a description of it.
practices.form: Storyboard (comic-strip customer journey), then interactive prototype, then observed user sessions
practices.decision_types: Expensive, uncertain bets that can be faked on the surface: new product, new market, big feature. One week; high stakes; reduces irreversibility before commitment.
practices.concrete_example: Their listed cases include Blue Bottle Coffee expanding into online sales and Savioke giving a hotel delivery robot a personality, each tested on a prototype before building.
practices.fails_when: The question is about back-end behavior that a surface facade cannot show, or the target customers are not recruited. Five interviews give qualitative signal, not statistics. It also fails when a single prototype invites inflated ratings (see Tohidi 2006).

practices.name: Apple demo-driven decisions ('creative selection')
practices.source: Ken Kocienda, Creative Selection: Inside Apple's Design Process During the Golden Age of Steve Jobs (book, 2018); quoted passages via a book summary
practices.what_is_shown: A concrete, specific, interactive demo of one narrow question, high fidelity inside a 'conceptual ring' around the key details and deliberately rough outside it. Reviewer reaction leads to the next demo. For variants, two demos can be switched between in the review.
practices.form: Interactive prototype (demo), reviewed live
practices.decision_types: Design and UX choices where feel matters and words are ambiguous: interaction, layout, defaults. Iterative, reversible, frequent; small to medium stakes each.
practices.concrete_example: The iPad keyboard demo: Jobs went back and forth between two keyboard options in the demo and asked to remove one. Kocienda reports this cascaded toward a simpler design.
practices.fails_when: One person's taste is the only oracle, so reactions are unpredictable and sometimes reversed days later (the author says so). Demos built at the wrong fidelity draw attention to the wrong details. It is not suited to decisions whose consequences appear only at scale or over time.

practices.name: Parallel alternatives before feedback (parallel prototyping)
practices.source: Dow, Glassco, Kass, Schwarz, Schwartz & Klemmer, ACM TOCHI 17(4) 2010
practices.what_is_shown: Several distinct alternatives are created and put side by side before any critique, instead of one option refined serially with feedback after each version.
practices.form: Multiple prototypes or options shown together
practices.decision_types: Design choices with a large solution space; avoiding fixation on the first option; medium stakes.
practices.concrete_example: Present three different shapes for the 'decision card' (one-line, one-screen, full page) side by side before asking which to refine, instead of polishing the first one.
practices.fails_when: The alternatives are trivially different, which gives no real contrast. Evidence comes from novice designers making web ads, measured by click-through and expert ratings; transfer to executive decisions is untested.

practices.name: Show three alternatives, not one, to get honest criticism (testing many vs one)
practices.source: Tohidi, Buxton, Baecker & Sellen, 'Getting the Right Design and the Design Right: Testing Many Is Better Than One', CHI 2006 (Microsoft Research)
practices.what_is_shown: Three functionally equivalent but stylistically distinct designs evaluated together, instead of one design alone.
practices.form: Multiple prototypes side by side
practices.decision_types: Evaluating a proposal with stakeholders or users when the evaluators may be polite or anchored on 'the' proposal.
practices.concrete_example: Instead of asking 'do you like this plan?', show plan A, plan B and plan C together; criticism of the favored plan becomes sharper and ratings more calibrated.
practices.fails_when: The goal is constructive redesign suggestions: even with multiple designs, end users identified problems but did not supply solutions. A single design shown alone received significantly higher ratings and less negative feedback, which is inflated.

practices.name: Joint evaluation: show options side by side so hard-to-evaluate attributes become visible
practices.source: Hsee, Blount, Loewenstein & Bazerman, 'Preference Reversals Between Joint and Separate Evaluations of Options', Psychological Bulletin 125(5) 1999; Hsee 1996 evaluability hypothesis
practices.what_is_shown: All options in one comparison table versus each option judged alone.
practices.form: Table (side-by-side comparison)
practices.decision_types: Choices between options where the important attribute is hard to judge in isolation (numbers without a reference point: entries, latency, cost per task).
practices.concrete_example: Music dictionary study: in joint evaluation the 20,000-entry dictionary with a torn cover got higher willingness to pay. Alone, the 10,000-entry 'like new' one won, because '20,000 entries' means nothing without a comparison.
practices.fails_when: The decider will actually experience the option alone (separate evaluation is closer to how it will feel). Joint view then over-weights attributes that are easy to compare but matter little in use. Evaluability can also be supplied by a reference point instead of a second option.

practices.name: Before/after journey maps (current-state then future-state)
practices.source: Kate Kaplan, Nielsen Norman Group, 'Journey-Mapping Approaches: 2 Critical Decisions To Make Before You Begin'
practices.what_is_shown: First a current-state map: steps, thoughts, emotions, pain points, frequency and magnitude of pain. Then a future-state map: the ideal journey used as a North Star and a feature-priority roadmap. NN/g recommends the hybrid order: assumption map, then research, then current state, then future state.
practices.form: Diagram (timeline of steps with emotional curve and pain points)
practices.decision_types: Investment and priority decisions about an experience or process; persuading stakeholders a problem exists; aligning a team on a target. Medium stakes, multi-step processes.
practices.concrete_example: Current: owner gets a 40-line wall of text from an agent, scrolls, asks 3 follow-up questions, decides 2 hours later. Future: owner sees the card, opens one case, taps a button in 2 minutes.
practices.fails_when: The process stops at an assumption-based hypothesis map that is never validated and then drives critical decisions. A future-state map without a current-state baseline gives no way to judge improvement.

practices.name: Military COA decision briefing after war-gaming (action-reaction-counteraction)
practices.source: US Army, Center for Army Lessons Learned handbook 23-07 'Military Decision-Making Process' (Nov 2023), citing FM 5-0 Planning and Orders Production (2022)
practices.what_is_shown: Before the briefing, each course of action (COA) is war-gamed turn by turn: action, enemy reaction, friendly counteraction, recorded on a synchronization matrix or sketch notes. The briefing then shows: higher commander's intent; status of forces; current intelligence picture; for each COA the assumptions, concept, war-game results, modifications, evaluation-criteria results, advantages and disadvantages including risks; then the recommended COA, with disagreement surfaced explicitly.
practices.form: Text structure / briefing plus decision matrix; war game as a tabletop simulation (belt, avenue-in-depth, box methods)
practices.decision_types: High stakes, adversarial, time-pressured choices among 2-3 alternatives. Scales down: the handbook notes that a single directed COA is used under time constraints.
practices.concrete_example: Each COA is played out against the enemy's likely response before the commander sees it, so the briefing reports 'COA 2 fails at phase II when the enemy reserve counterattacks', not just a list of pros and cons.
practices.fails_when: War-gaming is used to finish an incomplete plan instead of testing a complete one (the handbook warns against this). The staff cannot agree and hides it. It is too heavy for small reversible decisions.

practices.name: Shell decision scenarios (several coherent futures, including a surprise-free one)
practices.source: Pierre Wack, 'Scenarios: Uncharted Waters Ahead', Harvard Business Review, Sept-Oct 1985
practices.what_is_shown: First the predetermined elements (things already set in motion). Then several internally consistent stories of how the uncertain elements could unfold. One is 'surprise-free', matching managers' implicit view so they recognize their outlook. Then the implications of each for the decision at hand.
practices.form: Narrative scenarios (stories of alternative futures) with supporting quantification
practices.decision_types: Long-horizon strategic decisions under deep uncertainty where forecasting fails; irreversible capital commitments.
practices.concrete_example: Shell's 1970s package (four scenarios) prepared management for the eventuality, if not the timing, of the 1973 oil crisis. In 1981 Shell sold off excess oil before the glut.
practices.fails_when: Scenarios merely quantify alternative outcomes of obvious uncertainties ('oil at $20 or $40'); Wack calls these 'first-generation' and says they are not helpful to decision makers. A package with no surprise-free scenario feels alien and is rejected. Scenarios that do not change the decision makers' mental model ('microcosm') have no effect.

practices.name: Review the work-in-progress itself with advisors who have no authority (Pixar Braintrust and dailies)
practices.source: Ed Catmull, 'How Pixar Fosters Collective Creativity', HBR Sept 2008
practices.what_is_shown: The current version of the actual work: story reels (storyboards cut with temporary dialogue and music), or incomplete daily animation. A two-hour candid discussion follows. The director alone decides what to use; notes are not mandatory. Postmortems list the top five things to repeat and the top five not to, plus rework data.
practices.form: Example/case: the artifact itself (storyboard reel, unfinished work) shown, followed by discussion
practices.decision_types: Iterative creative or product quality decisions over a long project; reversible; the owner keeps authority.
practices.concrete_example: The Toy Story 2 reels were not improving; reviewing them led to new leads, who added 'Jessie's story' so the audience believed Woody had a real choice.
practices.fails_when: Reviewers are given authority: Catmull reports that the model did not work in the technical area until it was declared 'purely peers giving feedback'. Postmortems repeated in the same format find the same lessons.

practices.name: Figma critique formats: context, 'feedback I want / don't want', then structured feedback
practices.source: Noah Levin, Figma Blog, 'How we do design critiques at Figma'
practices.date: 2019 (blog; date approximate, not shown on page)
practices.what_is_shown: Standard crit: project context and goals (10-15 min), with a slide on 'feedback I'm looking for' and 'what I'm NOT looking for'; clarifying questions (2-5 min); feedback round-the-room or popcorn. Variants: silent critique (everyone comments in the file asynchronously), pair critique, print-out wall, jams, FYI.
practices.form: Facilitated meeting structure; artifact shown live or in a shared file
practices.decision_types: Feedback on design work in progress. Explicitly not for major product or roadmap decisions, which Figma keeps in a separate forum.
practices.concrete_example: The 'Comments in Figma' jam: a file with prompt questions ('should comments behave like email or Slack?'); six people drop references for 30 minutes, then discuss.
practices.fails_when: Rooms are overcrowded, problems are too complex for the time slot, feedback is shallow or '+1' groupthink, or popcorn mode lets the loudest voice win. It is not a decision forum by Figma's own definition.

principles: Concrete beats abstract only when it is the right concrete: a worked example helps novices (worked-example effect) but becomes redundant and harmful for experts (expertise reversal). Adapt depth to how familiar the decider is with this decision type.

One case is weak; two contrasting cases with an explicit 'what do they share' prompt transfer the principle (40% vs 22% in teams, 58% vs 24% individually). Studying cases separately was no better than no training. Show pairs and ask for the comparison.

A single vivid case moves decisions more than statistics, and adding statistics can cut the case's pull without adding theirs (Rokia $2.38 vs $1.43). Every case shown must come with its base rate or reference class, or it will distort.
Description of averages hides spread and makes outcomes look more predictable than they are, even to experts. Show individual outcomes (dots, sampled runs), not only the mean line or a coefficient.
For uncertain, complex outcomes, letting the decider 'live through' simulated outcomes beats both text and static charts. For simple problems, description is enough and cheaper.

Show the baseline story first ('how it is today', one specific case of the status quo failing), then the proposed future, so the solution can be judged against the problem (Shape Up, PR/FAQ, current vs future journey maps).
Before asking for approval, show the outside view: the distribution of similar past cases, then where this one sits (reference class forecasting).

Present alternatives together, not one at a time: single options get inflated ratings and weaker criticism (Tohidi 2006), joint evaluation makes hard-to-judge attributes meaningful (Hsee), and parallel options beat serial refinement (Dow 2010).

For irreversible or high-stakes plans, add a failure story in the past tense (premortem) after the plan: it reliably lowers overconfidence more than pros/cons or critique. Its effect on decision quality is unproven.

Match the fidelity of the example to the question: high detail only on the 'linchpin' part, deliberately rough elsewhere (Shape Up fat-marker sketches, Kocienda's 'conceptual ring'), or reviewers argue about irrelevant detail.
Separate the forum that gives feedback from the person who decides: advisors without authority speak more candidly (Pixar Braintrust), and critique formats are explicitly not decision forums (Figma).
Narratives in high-stakes decision aids are not recommended as a required component (IPDAS 2021). If used, prefer process and experience stories balanced across options over outcome testimonials.

Decision briefings that work list, per option: assumptions, how it played out in a simulated run (war game), criteria results, advantages and disadvantages including risk, then the recommendation, with disagreement surfaced (Army COA briefing).
numbers: Analogical encoding (Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner 2003): teams comparing two cases formed contingent contracts in 40% (24/60) of negotiations vs 22% (8/37) for separate-case study and 23% (50/213) for no training. Individuals in earlier studies: 58% (47/81) vs 24% (20/83). Comparison contracts had higher joint value: $4.76M vs $4.28M vs $4.19M.

Premortem (Veinott, Klein & Wiggins 2010, n=178): confidence change -25.0 points for premortem vs -14.0 pro/con, -12.4 cons-only, about 0 for critique and baseline. Premortem also had the largest rebound after generating fixes.

The widely quoted 'prospective hindsight improves identification of reasons by 30%' traces to Mitchell, Russo & Pennington 1989. Veinott et al. describe it as about 30% more reasons generated when the outcome is framed as certain, not as more accurate reasons. The 1989 abstract itself reports effects on explanation type, not accuracy.

Identifiable victim (Small, Loewenstein & Slovic 2007, Study 3, n=159): mean donation $2.38 for an identifiable victim, $1.14 for statistical victims, $1.43 for identifiable victim plus statistics. In Study 1, identifiable/no intervention was $2.83 vs $1.26 in the other three cells.

Illusion of predictability (Soyer & Hogarth 2012): 257 economics scholars misjudged outcome predictability from a standard regression description. Replacing the description with a scatter illustration produced accurate judgments.
Testing many vs one (Tohidi et al. 2006): a design shown alone got significantly higher ratings and less negative feedback than the same design shown among three alternatives.
Reference class (Flyvbjerg 2006): for 172 UK-comparable road projects, 40% overran cost by at most 10% and 80% by at most 32%. Rail and bridges/tunnels carried higher risk.
Hsee music-dictionary study: the 20,000-entry dictionary with a torn cover won in joint evaluation; the 10,000-entry like-new one won in separate evaluation.

PR/FAQ meetings (Amazon, per Bryar & Carr): 15-20 minutes of silent reading, then about 40 minutes of discussion; first draft should take hours, not days; AWS PR/FAQs took more than a year (2004 to 2006 launch).
Figma critiques: maximum two topics per one-hour crit; topics 'always take at least 10 minutes more than people think'.
not_found: Linear: no primary source found on how Linear runs product or design reviews; not searched in depth.
Apple design reviews beyond Kocienda's book: no first-party Apple source found. The Kocienda material was read via a book summary site that quotes the book, not the book itself.

Truong, Hayes & Abowd 2006 'Storyboarding: an empirical determination of best practices' (DIS 2006): found the citation, but the ACM page and Semantic Scholar were blocked (cookie wall, bot check), so its findings were not verified.
Klein's HBR 2007 premortem full text: paywalled on hbr.org. A course-hosted PDF copy was blocked by the permission system, so it was not read; the method steps are taken from Veinott et al. 2010.
Hogarth & Soyer 2011/2015 full papers: only abstracts and the MIT SMR summary were read; effect sizes for simulated experience were not extracted.
Shaffer et al. 2021 and Bekker et al. 2013: the 2021 abstract and recommendation sections were read; the 2013 PMC page returned only a title.

No controlled study found that directly compares 'one-line question plus recommendation plus buttons' against richer case-based decision presentations for software or agent workflows. All evidence above is from adjacent domains (education, negotiation, medicine, forecasting, design).
Sweller & Cooper 1985 original paper not opened; the worked-example effect is cited via the MIT TLL summary and Kalyuga 2001/2003 records.
Search was done via fetchira with the serper provider only; exa was not used (out of credits).

practices.name: Risk-tiered gating: auto-allow the safe, classify the middle, escalate only on repeated denials
practices.source: Anthropic, 'How we built Claude Code auto mode'
practices.date: 2026 (post undated on page; arXiv stress-test of it is 2604.04978)
practices.what_is_shown: The human sees nothing for tier 1 (read-only tools, user allow-rules) or tier 2 (in-project edits, reviewable via git). Tier 3 actions (shell, web, external tools, outside-project writes) go to a classifier, not a human. A blocked action goes back to the agent with a reason, and it tries a safer path. The human gets pulled in only after 3 consecutive or 20 total denials in a session.
practices.form: No per-action UI. Policy text (environment trust boundary, block rules, allow exceptions) that the user edits, plus an escalation interrupt.
practices.decision_types: High-volume, mostly reversible, low-to-medium stakes actions where per-action human review has turned into a formality. Not a replacement for careful review of high-stakes infrastructure.
practices.concrete_example: An agent hits an auth error and starts grepping env files for other tokens. The classifier blocks it as credential exploration. The agent asks or finds another route. The human is not interrupted unless blocks keep piling up.
practices.fails_when: Consent is ambiguous. 17% false-negative rate on real overeager actions: the classifier sees the danger but takes earlier approval-shaped words ('clean up the PR') as consent for a bigger blast radius. A similar earlier approval is wrongly treated as a pattern.

practices.name: Supervise by monitoring and interrupting, not by approving every step
practices.source: Anthropic, 'Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice'
practices.what_is_shown: A live view of what the agent is doing and a cheap way to interrupt or redirect it, instead of a gate on every action. The agent also stops by itself: it presents a choice between approaches (35% of its self-stops), gathers diagnostics (21%), clarifies a vague request (13%), asks for credentials (12%) or asks for approval before acting (11%).
practices.form: Streaming activity view with an interrupt/steer control, plus agent-initiated questions
practices.decision_types: Long, multi-step tasks by an experienced operator with outputs that can be tested (code). Less proven where checking the work takes the same expertise as doing it.
practices.concrete_example: New users (<50 sessions) use full auto-approve in about 20% of sessions, rising to over 40% by 750 sessions. Interrupt rate rises from 5% to 9% of turns at the same time, so oversight shifts from gating to watching.
practices.fails_when: The person is not actually watching, or the agent does not stop at the right moments. Anthropic warns that mandating approve-every-action adds friction 'without necessarily producing safety benefits'.

practices.name: Approve / edit / reject-with-feedback / respond decision set per gated tool
practices.source: LangChain docs, Human-in-the-loop middleware
practices.what_is_shown: An action request: tool name, exact arguments, a description, and the decisions allowed for this tool. Conditional 'when' predicates mean the reviewer sees only calls that need a decision. Rejection carries a message telling the agent whether to abandon, ask, or try a safer route.
practices.form: Structured interrupt (JSON schema per decision), rendered by any frontend as a card. Batched (one list per model turn) or per-call.
practices.decision_types: Side-effecting tool calls where the human may want to fix a parameter rather than just say yes or no (recipient, path, SQL)
practices.concrete_example: write_file is gated only for paths outside /workspace/. execute_sql is gated only when it is not a SELECT, and allows approve/reject but no edit. The reviewer edits the path to archive/orders_2024.csv and approves.
practices.fails_when: Large edits make the model re-plan and repeat actions. Batched mode needs answers in exact order. A 'respond' used to deny an action reads to the model as success.

practices.name: Agent policy pre-sorts the queue into ready-to-approve / needs-review / ready-to-reject, with cited rationale
practices.source: Ramp Support, 'Use Policy Agent for approvals'
practices.what_is_shown: The home page splits items into three sections by the agent's recommendation. Each item's activity feed shows the recommendation, the agent's rationale with the cited policy text, the policy version used, updated assessments when new info arrives, reviewer overrides and thumbs up/down. Clearly in-policy items under a threshold are auto-approved and never shown.
practices.form: Sectioned list (bulk-actionable) plus a per-item activity feed with citations
practices.decision_types: High-volume, repetitive, policy-checkable approvals with low per-item stakes (expenses, spend). Ambiguous policy routes to 'Requires review'.
practices.concrete_example: Auto-approve in-policy expenses under $1,000. A laptop accessory bought on a non-IT card shows as 'Rejection recommended', citing the policy sentence that requires the IT Procurement card.
practices.fails_when: The written policy is ambiguous or out of sync with deterministic settings. The bulk 'ready to approve' section invites rubber-stamping of the agent's own recommendations.

practices.name: Review queue: scannable list first, risk insights and related items on drill-down, prev/next navigation
practices.source: Stripe Docs, 'Review payments' (Radar)
practices.what_is_shown: List view: risk level, customer, payment method, amount, date. Detail view: the top risk factors behind the score, related payments sharing email/IP/card, and merchant-supplied metadata (order, shipping, a Street View link). Actions: Approve, Refund, Refund and report fraud. The review timeline records each action.
practices.form: Two-level list/detail queue with Previous/Next to move through items
practices.decision_types: Items where human judgment adds information the model lacks. Stripe says to send only cases 'where the benefit is clear' to humans.
practices.concrete_example: A high-risk order from abroad. The reviewer sees 'card used with 3 emails in 24h' among the risk insights and a freight-forwarder address in Street View, then refunds and reports fraud.
practices.fails_when: Everything is routed to review (bottleneck). The business has no natural delay, so review slows good customers. Refund is irreversible.

practices.name: Specific confirmation: restate the exact object and consequence, with labeled outcome buttons
practices.source: Jakob Nielsen, NN/g, 'Confirmation Dialogs Can Prevent User Errors — If Not Overused'
practices.what_is_shown: What exactly will happen, to which named objects and how many (for example, list name plus subscriber count). Buttons name the outcome ('Delete file' / 'Keep file'). 'Tell me more' details sit behind progressive disclosure. No default Yes.
practices.form: Short text dialog, outcome-labeled buttons, optional expand. Typed confirmation for the rarest, most dangerous cases.
practices.decision_types: Irreversible or costly actions only. Never routine ones. Thresholds can be personal (for example, payments at least twice the user's usual amount).
practices.concrete_example: MailChimp makes the user type DELETE before removing a list and shows the list name and subscriber count.
practices.fails_when: Used for routine actions (cry-wolf). Vague text like 'these 2 items'. Typed confirmations used often enough to become a new automatic habit.

practices.name: Remove the confirmation instead: undo, assume-and-make-changeable, bulk 'apply to all', postpone exceptions to the end
practices.source: Microsoft Windows UX guidelines, Confirmations
practices.what_is_shown: Ideally nothing. If a confirmation stays, it carries all the information needed to answer and the reason not to proceed ('... anyway' button labels). Bulk operations get one 'apply to all' choice, or exceptions are collected and shown at the end.
practices.form: Design rule set (when to cut a prompt), plus the dialog text structure: main instruction, supplemental reason, specific commit buttons
practices.decision_types: Frequent actions. Rule: if one response is chosen about 98% of the time, remove the confirmation (security, legal and safety are possible exceptions).
practices.concrete_example: Instead of asking about each read-only file during a bulk move, move them and present the leftover conflicts in one confirmation at the end.
practices.fails_when: No real undo exists. Teams add a 'don't show again' box to keep an unnecessary prompt alive.

practices.name: Context-rich push approval with number matching (anti-fatigue)
practices.source: Microsoft Entra Blog (Alex Weinert), 'Defend your users from MFA fatigue attacks'
practices.what_is_shown: Instead of a bare 'Approve?' push: the requesting app, the IP-based location, and a two-digit code that the approver must type from the originating screen.
practices.form: Mobile push notification plus a typed challenge
practices.decision_types: Frequent, security-relevant one-tap approvals that an attacker (or a runaway agent) can trigger repeatedly
practices.concrete_example: Microsoft: about 1% of users accept a simple approval request on the first try. In live customer environments, number matching plus additional context 'eliminated MFA fatigue attacks when enabled'.
practices.fails_when: Applied to every low-risk approval, where it becomes friction. The approver has no independent view of the originating context to check against.

practices.name: Polymorphic (changing-appearance) warnings against habituation
practices.source: Vance, Jenkins, Anderson, Bjornn, Kirwan, 'Tuning Out Security Warnings' (MIS Quarterly 42(2))
practices.what_is_shown: The same risk information, but the visual presentation varies between exposures, so the brain does not filter it out as familiar
practices.form: Visual variation of a warning or approval card (layout, color, element order)
practices.decision_types: Rare high-risk prompts mixed into a stream of routine ones
practices.concrete_example: fMRI and eye-tracking over a five-day week showed attention to warnings declining, with partial recovery between days. In a 3-week field study of mobile permission prompts, adherence dropped substantially for standard warnings but stayed high for polymorphic ones.
practices.fails_when: Variation is used on routine prompts (it becomes noise and erodes trust). Variation replaces specificity and fewer prompts instead of adding to them.

practices.name: Alert override data as a warning: most clinical alerts are overridden
practices.source: Nanji et al., 'Overrides of medication-related clinical decision support alerts in outpatients', JAMIA 21(3):487-91 (summary via AHRQ PSNet)
practices.what_is_shown: (Anti-pattern) Interruptive alerts during order entry, many low-value, shown with the same weight as critical ones
practices.form: Modal interruptive alert
practices.decision_types: Shows what happens when every check interrupts a busy expert
practices.concrete_example: About 53% of outpatient alerts were overridden, and half of those should have been addressed. Other studies report 73-96% override rates (Poly 2020: 96.2%).
practices.fails_when: This is the failure case: undifferentiated alert volume trains experts to click through. The finding parallels Anthropic's 93% prompt-acceptance figure.

practices.name: Confirm before state-changing actions, with watch mode for sensitive sites
practices.source: OpenAI, Operator System Card
practices.what_is_shown: A chat message that states the prepared action in final form ('I've drafted the email to X requesting a password reset. Would you like me to send it?'), with a screenshot of the staged state. On high-risk sites (email), execution pauses when the user looks away. A prompt-injection monitor pauses and explains why.
practices.form: Conversational confirmation plus a screenshot of the staged state; pause/resume banner
practices.decision_types: Irreversible or world-affecting steps in otherwise delegated tasks: purchases, sending email, bulk deletes. Highest-risk tasks (stock trading, banking) are refused outright.
practices.concrete_example: On 100 unmitigated tasks there were 13 errors, 5 of them irreversible (wrong email recipient, bulk label removal). Confirmations cut this risk by about 90%. Confirmation recall is 92% on 607 risky tasks.
practices.fails_when: The model misses a confirmation (8% of cases). The user confirms from the summary without opening the staged artifact.

practices.name: Interruption levels and scheduled summary delivery
practices.source: Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Managing notifications
practices.what_is_shown: Each notification is tagged passive / active / time-sensitive / critical. Only time-sensitive and critical break through Focus and the scheduled summary. Everything else is batched into a summary at times the user picks. The system periodically asks the user whether an app's time-sensitive alerts are earning that level.
practices.form: OS-level notification channels plus a periodic digest
practices.decision_types: Separates decisions that expire within about an hour (interrupt now) from ones that can wait for a batch review
practices.concrete_example: An agent's 'deploy waiting, window closes in 40 min' is time-sensitive. 'Three draft posts ready for review' is passive and lands in the evening summary.
practices.fails_when: An app over-labels urgency. Users then turn time-sensitive off (Apple builds this demotion in) or turn off notifications entirely.

practices.name: Batch notifications three times a day
practices.source: Fitz, Kushlev, Jagannathan et al., 'Batching smartphone notifications can improve well-being', Computers in Human Behavior
practices.what_is_shown: Non-urgent items held and delivered in fixed batches rather than one by one
practices.form: Scheduled digest
practices.decision_types: Non-time-critical approvals for a single person facing many interruptions per day
practices.concrete_example: Field experiment: batching notifications three times a day reduced stress and raised well-being and perceived productivity. Turning alerts off completely raised anxiety and fear of missing out.
practices.fails_when: A truly time-critical decision is caught in the batch. No batching at all, or total silence, both do worse.

practices.name: Summarize-then-group notifications; drop stale ones
practices.source: Material Design (M2), Android notifications platform guidance
practices.what_is_shown: A parent summary ('3 new messages') that expands to children. Each child must make sense alone. Title under 30 characters, text under 40 characters, at most 3 actions, which must not duplicate the tap action. Tapping opens the screen where the action happens. Notifications that are no longer relevant are dismissed automatically.
practices.form: Grouped push notifications with an expandable summary; importance channels (HIGH / DEFAULT / LOW / MIN)
practices.decision_types: Many same-type items from one source (an agent's pending approvals)
practices.concrete_example: 'Agent: 5 actions waiting' expands to five one-line children. Each has Approve / Open. An item already resolved on desktop disappears from the phone.
practices.fails_when: Unimportant items are disguised as urgent ('unnecessary alarm'). Stale cards remain and get approved after the situation has changed.

practices.name: Self-updating approval card: role-specific buttons, state written back after action
practices.source: Microsoft Teams docs, Universal Actions for Adaptive Cards: Up to date cards
practices.what_is_shown: Request title, who submitted it, whose approval is pending, who has already approved. Approve/Reject buttons appear only for the named approvers. After each action the card refreshes for everyone. The final state ('Approved by Nestor and Megan') replaces the buttons.
practices.form: Chat card (Adaptive Card) with refresh and user-specific views
practices.decision_types: Asynchronous approvals in a chat stream, including multi-approver ones
practices.concrete_example: An asset request B12 card shows 'Approval pending from Megan; approved by Nestor' with buttons only on Megan's view. After she approves, the buttons disappear for everyone.
practices.fails_when: Card state is not refreshed, so someone acts on an outdated card. The card carries only a title, so the approver decides without the details.

practices.name: Progressive disclosure in chat messages; clean up into a text record afterwards
practices.source: Slack Developer Docs, 'Designing with Block Kit'
practices.what_is_shown: Only what the current step needs. Secondary info goes into context blocks, rarely used options into an overflow menu. A sensible default reduces the choice to yes/no (for example, reorder the last order). Once resolved, the message is condensed to a short record of what happened. Charts come with an accessible data table.
practices.form: Chat message blocks: header, section, context, buttons, overflow; later edited into a plain record
practices.decision_types: Light, frequent decisions in a chat surface, with the default being the most likely answer
practices.concrete_example: A coffee bot shows 'Same as last time: oat flat white?' with Yes/No. After the tap, the message becomes 'Ordered oat flat white, 9:12'.
practices.fails_when: The default answer is wrong for a risky action (it invites one-tap acceptance). Buttons remain after expiry and get pressed later.

practices.name: Mobile review surface: description in header, status at a glance, merge in place when checks pass
practices.source: GitHub Changelog, 'Working with pull requests on GitHub Mobile is now much easier'
practices.what_is_shown: Order: PR description in the header (long text truncated, expands inline), then a merge box summarizing reviews, checks and mergeability with color and icons, then a Files Changed cell saying whether your review is needed or new changes arrived since your last review. Merge is possible right there when everything passes.
practices.form: Mobile detail screen with a status summary and an inline expandable description
practices.decision_types: Approve or merge decisions where automated checks carry most of the verification and the human checks intent
practices.concrete_example: An agent's PR on the phone: header 'Fix timezone parsing in reminders', checks green, '2 new commits since your review', Merge button.
practices.fails_when: Large diffs. SmartBear/Cisco data show review effectiveness drops beyond 200-400 LOC or above about 500 LOC/hour, and a phone pushes reviewers toward exactly that speed.

practices.name: Default human gate on agent-triggered side effects, removable per repository
practices.source: GitHub Changelog, 'Optionally skip approval for Copilot coding agent Actions workflows'
practices.what_is_shown: The agent's PR is treated like one from an outside contributor. CI workflows (which may access secrets) wait for an 'Approve and run workflows' button in the merge box. Admins can turn the gate off per repository.
practices.form: Single button in the PR merge box; repository setting
practices.decision_types: A gate on one boundary-crossing step (secrets, CI tokens) rather than on every agent action
practices.concrete_example: Copilot pushes a change. Tests stay pending until a maintainer glances at workflow file changes and presses 'Approve and run workflows'.
practices.fails_when: The button is pressed without inspecting workflow changes (it slows the feedback loop, so people stamp it). The gate is turned off in repos with powerful secrets.

practices.name: Mobile incident triage: urgency-sorted queue, act from notification, stateful color
practices.source: PagerDuty Docs, 'PagerDuty Mobile App'
practices.what_is_shown: The push shows incident number, service and description, with Ack available from the notification itself. The list sorts by urgency, priority or recency. Banner color shows state (red triggered, yellow acknowledged). The detail view has Triage (actions) and Overview (impacted service, responders, latest status, timeline, triggered alerts, past and related incidents) tabs.
practices.form: Push notification with quick action; swipe actions in a list; tabbed detail
practices.decision_types: Time-critical, reversible first responses (ack, snooze, escalate). Deeper decisions are made in detail view.
practices.concrete_example: Long-press the push and tap Ack to stop escalation. Later, open Overview, see related past incidents, then Resolve.
practices.fails_when: Low-urgency events use high-urgency channels (the alert-fatigue pattern). Acking from the lock screen becomes a reflex that stops escalation without anyone working the incident.

practices.name: Triage inbox with single-key decisions and snooze-until-activity
practices.source: Linear Docs, Triage
practices.what_is_shown: A separate inbox for incoming items from integrations and outsiders. Each item: accept (1), decline (2), mark duplicate (3), snooze (H). Snooze returns the item at a chosen time or on new activity. Rules and an AI agent pre-fill assignee and labels and flag likely duplicates.
practices.form: Keyboard-driven inbox queue with automation rules
practices.decision_types: Many small accept/decline/route decisions per day by one owner
practices.concrete_example: An agent-proposed task lands in triage with 'likely duplicate of X' suggested. The owner presses 3 and merges, or presses H to revisit when the agent posts new info.
practices.fails_when: Items that need a deep look get the same one-key treatment. Pre-filled suggestions get accepted without a check.

principles: Cut the number of prompts before improving any single prompt. Microsoft's test: if one answer is chosen about 98% of the time, remove the confirmation. Ask for a human decision only where a 'no' is realistic.

Tier by reversibility and blast radius. Reversible, in-scope actions run unasked (undo or git is the safety net). Boundary-crossing or irreversible actions (secrets, external send, deletes, prod) get a gate (Anthropic auto mode tiers, GitHub Copilot workflow gate, OpenAI Operator policy).
Make every approval specific: name the exact object, count and consequence, and label buttons with outcomes ('Send to 3 recipients' / 'Keep draft'), not 'Approve' / 'OK' (NN/g, Microsoft).
Show the decision in final staged form (the drafted email, the selected items, the diff) rather than a description of intent (Operator confirmations).

Put the recommendation and its cited reason first, the evidence one tap away. Three buckets work for queues: ready to approve / needs review / ready to reject (Ramp). Top risk factors plus related items work for drill-down (Stripe).
Use progressive disclosure: a short headline and action on the card, details behind expand. Never hide information the person needs to answer (Microsoft, Slack, Material).

Separate urgency honestly. Only decisions that expire within about an hour may interrupt. Everything else goes into 2-3 daily batches. Over-labelling urgency gets the channel muted (Apple HIG, Fitz 2019).

Defend against habituation in rare high-stakes prompts: add context and a non-standard action (type a code or word), and consider varying the appearance. Use these only for the rare prompts, or they become new habits (Microsoft number matching, Vance 2018, NN/g).
Allow edit and reject-with-reason, not only yes/no. The reason goes back to the agent so it can choose a safer path instead of stalling (LangChain HITL, Anthropic deny-and-continue).
Keep cards live: refresh state after any action, show who decided, collapse to a text record when done, and auto-dismiss stale requests (Teams, Slack, Material).

Size the reviewable unit. Human verification degrades past about 200-400 LOC or about 60 minutes. Split large agent outputs or rely on automated checks plus a human intent check (SmartBear/Cisco, GitHub mobile merge box).

Measure the gate itself: approval rate, override rate, time-to-decide, and later-reversed approvals. A gate approved over 90% of the time is a formality and should be automated or redesigned (Anthropic 93%, clinical alert override data).
numbers: 93%: share of Claude Code permission prompts users approve (Anthropic auto mode post, 2026)

Auto mode classifier: 0.4% false-positive rate on 10,000 real tool calls; 17% false-negative rate on 52 real overeager actions; 5.7% FNR on 1,000 synthetic exfiltration attempts. Stage 1 alone: 8.5% FPR, 6.6% FNR (Anthropic)
Auto mode escalates to the human after 3 consecutive or 20 total denials in a session (Anthropic)
Full auto-approve: about 20% of sessions for new users (<50 sessions), over 40% by 750 sessions. Interrupt rate rises from 5% to 9% of turns with experience (Anthropic, 2026-02-18)

Claude Code self-stops: 35% to present a choice of approaches, 21% for diagnostics, 13% to clarify, 12% for credentials or access, 11% for approval before acting. Human interrupts: 32% to provide missing context or corrections (Anthropic, 2026-02-18)
Internal Claude Code: human interventions per session fell from 5.4 to 3.3 (Aug-Dec) while success on the hardest tasks doubled (Anthropic)
Only 0.8% of API agent actions appear irreversible; 73% appear to have a human in the loop; 80% have some safeguard (Anthropic)
Operator: 13 errors on 100 unmitigated tasks, 5 irreversible. Confirmations reduced this risk by about 90%. Confirmation recall 92% on 607 risky tasks (OpenAI, 2025-01-23)
About 1% of users accept a simple MFA approval request on the first try. Number matching plus context 'eliminated MFA fatigue attacks when enabled' in live environments (Microsoft, 2022-09-28)
About 53% of outpatient medication alerts overridden, half of which should have been addressed (Nanji et al., JAMIA 2014). Other studies report 64% (ED) to 96.2% override rates
Batching notifications 3 times a day reduced stress and raised well-being. Turning all alerts off increased anxiety (Fitz et al., 2019)
Code review: 200-400 LOC per session over 60-90 minutes yields 70-90% defect discovery; effectiveness drops above about 500 LOC/hour or after about 60 minutes (SmartBear/Cisco)
Android notification text limits: title under 30 characters, content under 40 characters, at most 3 actions (Material M2)
Apple: time-sensitive notifications are for events happening now or within an hour
